Two high-profile animal hoarding cases in Martin County this summer — and a third in Palm Beach County — have prompted questions about whether more can be done to prevent animal neglect before it reaches a crisis point. The answers, experts say, are not simple.On July 20, Martin County deputies rescued more than 100 cats and dogs from a house near Hobe Sound.WATCH BELOW: Animal hoarding cases raise questions about prevention efforts"This is the worst animal hoarding case that I've seen," Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the scene.Exactly three weeks later, on Aug. 10, the same group of deputies rescued 36 border collies from a Palm City house piled with feces and rot. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, which was still handling rescue efforts of the previous case, then said this was the worst hoarding case they'd ever seen.On Sept. 16, Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputies, serving an unrelated arrest warrant near Lantana, rescued 13 dogs from another feces-filled home. According to the affidavit, seven of the dogs were confined inside 2 cages.Cesar Perea, vice president of the American Humane Society, said cases like these are not unusual."Unfortunately, it's really common throughout the country to see this level of neglect going on," Perea said.When asked why it is so common, Perea pointed to intent gone wrong."It's typically well-intentioned, whether it's a breeding operation or a rescue operation that just eventually just goes wrong," Perea said.The American Humane Society monitors cases like these across the U.S. and assists law enforcement and local animal rescues when called upon. Perea said he does not believe the number of cases is necessarily growing — but that public awareness is."I don't know if it's so much these cases are increasing. I think a lot of it has to do with awareness. I think with social media and people being involved, I think we're experiencing like a renaissance of people just not standing for it," Perea said.That shift in public attitude is reaching lawmakers, according to Kate MacFall, the Florida state director for Humane World for Animals. MacFall works in Tallahassee, where her job is to help shape Florida's animal welfare policy."Our legislators are filing more animal bills," MacFall said. "We've done a lot of really good things in recent years, but there's a lot of work to be done."But preventing hoarding cases specifically is more complicated."It's a bigger picture question," MacFall said.A major obstacle is the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures. Budensiek addressed the limitation when initially asked about the Border Collie case, after a neighbor raised concerns about the dogs at a WPTV Let's Hear It community meet-up."There's laws and case law that say you can go this far and you can go no further unless you have probable cause," Budensiek said.That constitutional boundary makes the problem difficult to address through legislation alone."A lot of times with legislation you create unintended consequences, so you have to be really careful," Perea said.For now, advocates say individual action remains the most effective tool."If you see something, say something. I mean, that's for a reason," MacFall said.Some policy efforts are in the works. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, has expressed interest in a mandatory breeder registry. In Palm Beach County, commissioners are expected to consider higher fees and mandatory inspections for hobby breeders later this fall.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Bob Pettit, an imposing scorer and rebounder for the St. Louis Hawks and winner of the NBA’s first Most Valuable Player award in 1956, has died. He was 93.Pettit's alma mater, LSU, announced Thursday that he died a day earlier. The university did not provide a cause of death.Pettit was an All-American at LSU before going on to the NBA, where he was an All-Star for each of his 11 seasons, all with the Hawks. He led them to the 1958 championship over the mighty Boston Celtics, the Hawks’ lone title.He was also the NBA MVP in 1959 and was the MVP of the All-Star game four times, an achievement matched only by Los Angeles Lakers great Kobe Bryant.Pettit was a force at a time when the NBA featured the likes of Wilt Chamberlain, Bill Russell, Oscar Robertson and Elgin Baylor. But it was also before a time when the NBA was widely seen on television, and Pettit — playing in a smaller market — was denied a larger audience.At 6-foot-9 and 205 pounds and with a deeply receding hairline, Pettit was a physical presence at power forward, before such a position became part of basketball’s vocabulary. He also played center and was one of the first big men who did not play solely with his back to the basket.Pettit was the Rookie of the Year in 1955, the last year the Hawks played in Milwaukee before moving to St. Louis.He captured the MVP the next season, leading the league in scoring at 25.7 points a game. He also was the NBA’s scoring leader in 1959 at 29.2 points.RELATED STORY | Former NBA player ejected from WNBA game after confrontation with Chicago playerHe retired after the 1964-65 season with career averages of 26.4 points and 16.2 rebounds. At that time, he was the NBA’s career leader in points (20,880) and second in rebounds (12,849).He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 1970.“Lean, graceful, and always well-conditioned, Bob Pettit's physical build made him one of the first big men to play facing the basket,” reads Pettit’s biographical profile at the Hall of Fame. “But Pettit's resolve set him apart from his peers; he simply would not be outworked.”Robert Lee Pettit Jr. 12, 1932, in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. His father worked in law enforcement and served as East Baton Rouge Parish Sheriff. Pettit was a late bloomer in basketball, not making the Baton Rouge High School varsity until his junior season.As a senior, he led Baton Rouge to a state championship and wound up with more than a dozen college offers. He chose to stay home and starred at LSU as a sophomore, an era when players could not join the varsity until then.He led the Southeastern Conference in scoring all three of his seasons, with averages of 25.5 points as a sophomore, 24.9 as a junior and 31.4 as a senior.Pettit is one of only three LSU players — Pete Maravich and Shaquille O’Neal the others — to earn a place in the Hall of Fame. Bronze statues of Pettit and O’Neal stand outside LSU’s home arena, the Pete Maravich Assembly Center. 50 is retired by LSU, his No. 9 by the Atlanta Hawks.“We are grateful for his contributions to our franchise and to basketball history,” the Hawks said in a statement. 9 jersey continues to hang proudly at State Farm Arena as a lasting reminder of the impact he made on our organization. We extend our deepest condolences to Bob’s family, friends and loved ones during this difficult time. We also join those across the basketball world in celebrating a remarkable life and legacy that will never be forgotten.”RELATED STORY | Clippers rocked by NBA punishment over salary cap circumvention schemePettit’s misfortune was that most of his career coincided with a run of Celtics championships that remains one of the most dominant runs in American pro sports history.Pettit was two victories short of being a three-time NBA champion. Pettit’s Hawks advanced to the finals four times, all against Boston, twice losing in seven games.The first meeting, won by Boston in 1957, came down to double overtime of Game 7. The second ended with a championship for the Hawks, interrupting Boston’s run of nine titles in 10 seasons. The Hawks also dropped NBA Finals matchups with the Celtics in 1960 (in seven games) and 1961 (in five).Pettit retired to his native Baton Rouge after leaving basketball and worked in banking and financial consulting. He was a regular at LSU and New Orleans Pelicans games in recent years.

Two West Palm Beach men have been arrested and charged with first-degree murder in connection with a 2019 homicide in Riviera Beach that had remained unsolved for years.Damien Dwayne King and Robert Rashad Pettway were arrested Wednesday on charges stemming from the shooting death of Kevin M. Ulysse, who was found fatally wounded in the roadway at 717 West 7th Street on Oct. 16, 2019.Police said the breakthrough came after the North Palm Beach Police Department's Cold Case Team took over the investigation in 2025, bringing fresh eyes to evidence that had gone cold.PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Man fatally shot in Riviera Beach in 2019Riviera Beach officers responded to reports of a shooting around 4:42 p.m. on that October afternoon and found Ulysse lying in the street with a gunshot wound. He was pronounced dead at the scene.Despite extensive efforts by Riviera Beach detectives — including witness interviews, physical evidence examination and pursuing investigative leads — no arrests were made at the time.The case was transferred to North Palm Beach Police in 2025 for an independent review. Police said the department's Cold Case Team conducted a comprehensive examination of the original investigation and developed new leads that eventually identified King and Pettway as suspects.On Sept. 23, 2026, arrest warrants were issued charging King with first-degree murder and attempted armed robbery. Pettway faces charges of first-degree murder, attempted robbery and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon.Police said King was arrested at his West Palm Beach residence by the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Pettway was apprehended through coordination between the sheriff's office fugitive warrants unit and West Palm Beach Police.Both police chiefs emphasized the importance of inter-agency collaboration in solving cold cases."This case demonstrates the power of partnership and persistence," said Riviera Beach Police Chief Michael A. "Our commitment to justice does not fade with time."North Palm Beach Police Chief Robert Coliskey added: "Revisiting cold cases with fresh eyes and shared resources can bring long-awaited closure to families. A 37-year-old man is facing charges after police say he was the aggressor in a confrontation that ended with him being shot at a Port St. Lucie restaurant Saturday afternoon.Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. 19 when a 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. Two high-profile animal hoarding cases in Martin County this summer — and a third in Palm Beach County — have prompted questions about whether more can be done to prevent animal neglect before it reaches a crisis point. The answers, experts say, are not simple. On July 20, Martin County deputies rescued more than 100 cats and dogs from a house near Hobe Sound. “This is the worst animal hoarding case that I’ve seen,” Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the scene. Exactly three weeks later, on Aug. 10, the same group of deputies rescued 36 border collies from a Palm City house piled with feces and rot. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, which was still handling rescue efforts of the previous case, then said this was the worst hoarding case they’d ever seen. 16, Palm Beach County Sheriff’s deputies, serving an unrelated arrest warrant near Lantana, rescued 13 dogs from another feces-filled home. According to the affidavit, seven of the dogs were confined inside 2 cages. Cesar Perea, vice president of the American Humane Society, said cases like these are not unusual. “Unfortunately, it’s really common throughout the country to see this level of neglect going on,” Perea said. When asked why it is so common, Perea pointed to intent gone wrong. “It’s typically well-intentioned, whether it’s a breeding operation or a rescue operation that just eventually just goes wrong,” Perea said. The American Humane Society monitors cases like these across the U.S. and assists law enforcement and local animal rescues when called upon. Perea said he does not believe the number of cases is necessarily growing — but that public awareness is. “I don’t know if it’s so much these cases are increasing. I think a lot of it has to do with awareness. I think with social media and people being involved, I think we’re experiencing like a renaissance of people just not standing for it,” Perea said. That shift in public attitude is reaching lawmakers, according to Kate MacFall, the Florida state director for Humane World for Animals. MacFall works in Tallahassee, where her job is to help shape Florida’s animal welfare policy. “Our legislators are filing more animal bills,” MacFall said. “We’ve done a lot of really good things in recent years, but there’s a lot of work to be done.” But preventing hoarding cases specifically is more complicated. “It’s a bigger picture question,” MacFall said. A major obstacle is the Fourth Amendment’s protection against unreasonable searches and seizures. Budensiek addressed the limitation when initially asked about the Border Collie case, after a neighbor raised concerns about the dogs at a WPTV Let’s Hear It community meet-up. “There’s laws and case law that say you can go this far and you can go no further unless you have probable cause,” Budensiek said. That constitutional boundary makes the problem difficult to address through legislation alone. “A lot of times with legislation you create unintended consequences, so you have to be really careful,” Perea said. For now, advocates say individual action remains the most effective tool. “If you see something, say something. I mean, that’s for a reason,” MacFall said. Some policy efforts are in the works. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, has expressed interest in a mandatory breeder registry. In Palm Beach County, commissioners are expected to consider higher fees and mandatory inspections for hobby breeders later this fall. World Market celebrated the grand opening of its Palm Beach Gardens location Friday, bringing its signature collection of globally-inspired home goods and international foods to South Florida. The new store at the Prosperity Centre shopping center represents a significant milestone for the California-based retailer, which has been planning and preparing for the opening in Palm Beach Gardens for two years."We are beyond excited to be here. It's been a long journey, but we are thrilled to be in the community," said Carrie Crooker, World Market's senior vice president of stores. Crooker, a 20-year veteran of the company, traveled to Palm Beach Gardens to personally oversee the launch of the new location.Among the eager customers lining up for the grand opening were Michael and Heather Sharin, local residents who live just over the bridge from the new shopping center."When we go to Tallahassee to visit our son, there's been a World Market there, and that's the first place I want to go," Heather Sharin said. "And when I heard it was coming here, well, here I am. It's opening day!"The decision to establish World Market's South Florida presence in Palm Beach Gardens was thanks to the welcoming community."This community is just an amazing, it has everything to offer," Crooker said. "It has diverse clientele here, lots of customers that have traveled all over the world that want to experience fun things. They are explorers and entertainers, and it fits our brand."For shoppers like the Sharins, World Market's appeal lies in its unique product mix that sets it apart from traditional retailers. "I like to look at things that are from all over the world," Heather said. "But also they have food, and they have beverages, and different kinds of drinks that I've never seen anywhere else. It has things that the other stores don't have."Michael Sharin echoed his wife's sentiment about the store's distinctive offerings. "It's not just a supermarket, it's not just a furniture store— It's the everything store," Michael said. The Palm Beach Gardens location transforms the former Office Depot space into World Market's signature shopping experience. "They will find a lot to explore. It's quite a treasure hunt here," Crooker explained, describing what first-time visitors can expect.The store features World Market's trademark international food department with products sourced from around the globe, alongside an extensive selection of furniture, home décor, and seasonal items. With Halloween and holiday merchandise already on display, the timing of the opening allows local shoppers to explore everything from harvest decorations to early holiday shopping options."So whether you are getting ready for a big Halloween party, getting ready for the fall and Thanksgiving, or you want to get some early shopping done for holiday, we're here for you," Crooker said.The arrival of World Market also contributes to the continued revitalization of the Prosperity Centre shopping plaza, including the opening of Plum Market next door in March. "I'm just happy because it makes this shopping center full again," Heather Sharin said. Friday's grand opening featured samples from around the world, giving visitors a taste of the international experience World Market brings to the Palm Beach Gardens community. The celebration marked not just the opening of a new retail location, but the arrival of a brand that Crooker believes fills a unique niche in the local market."We're here to bring something to Palm Beach Gardens that I think the community needs, and I think they are going to have so much fun in our stores," Crooker said.The Palm Beach Gardens store operates Monday through Saturday from 9:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m, and Sunday from 10 a.m.

Loved ones are grieving the loss of two young brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. The boys, 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark, grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt told WPBF 25 News that both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother also told WPBF 25 News they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the brothers' deaths. "Two children should still be alive today," Padrick said during a news conference. According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys told WPBF 25 News that the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident. Police said both survived and received treatment for their injuries. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday. "No family should have to endure the senseless loss of children," DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said. As the investigation continues in Georgia, the boys' family and members of the Fort Pierce community are focused on bringing them home to be laid to rest. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida. A year after WFLX first investigated a contentious legal battle over the future of Fisherman’s Wharf, newly released environmental testing is raising fresh questions about a key argument in the dispute: contamination. The city of Fort Pierce previously told developer Chris Shelli that the waterfront property at the center of his lawsuit was “likely contaminated” and suggested the cost of remediation could essentially eliminate his claim for damages. But the city made that assertion before the Florida Department of Environmental Protection had completed its testing. According to site assessments obtained by WFLX, FDEP found arsenic above state residential cleanup targets in two soil samples on city-owned land sold to Shelli. However, both samples were less than twice the residential cleanup target, and an environmental researcher who reviewed the findings for WFLX said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming. “I don’t think it’s necessarily something to be too concerned with,” said Jordon Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute. Shelli purchased approximately 3.2 acres around Fisherman’s Wharf with plans to transform the waterfront into a new destination. But WFLX Investigates previously uncovered a significant complication with the deal. Roughly half of the property was subject to a state right-of-reverter restriction, meaning the land could revert to the state if it were sold for private development. Emails obtained by WFLX in our first investigation showed Fort Pierce commissioners did not learn until 2023 — about two years after the sale — that removing the restriction could cost nearly $2 million. Shelli ultimately sued the city for breach of contract. In 2025, an attorney for the city sent Shelli a letter arguing the property was “likely contaminated” and that the cost of “remediation” essentially “eliminates” his damages claim. At the time, however, FDEP’s environmental investigation was still underway. The environmental concerns extend beyond the Fisherman’s Wharf property itself. Land immediately north of Fisherman’s Wharf was once home to a citrus packing house. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site — a designation used for property where redevelopment may be complicated by actual or perceived environmental contamination. FDEP’s site assessment found several soil samples at the former citrus packing house contained arsenic above Florida’s residential and industrial cleanup targets. Beckler said those findings were consistent with the property’s historical industrial use. “Personally, there’s not really much in the report that alarmed me,” Beckler said. “I think the findings are consistent with the past industrial uses of the site.” One sample, however, stood out. FDEP found an arsenic concentration roughly 148 times Florida’s residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of the former citrus packing house property. But that hot spot was not on the land sold to Shelli. Shelli’s proposed development property sits across the street. FDEP did send letters to seven surrounding property owners warning about possible off-site contamination. One of those letters went to the city of Fort Pierce and identified arsenic above the residential cleanup target in two soil samples on city-owned property sold to Shelli. Those exceedances, however, were far smaller than the hot spot found at the former packing house. Both were less than twice the residential cleanup target. Beckler also noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and that naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils. “The vast majority of those samples, while, yes, they were above that residential standard, they weren’t that high above it,” Beckler said. The distinction could become important in Shelli’s lawsuit. FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels included in its assessment, but those parcels are associated with the former citrus packing house property. The agency did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli. That is notable because the city’s earlier letter specifically cited “remediation” when arguing that contamination would essentially eliminate Shelli’s damages. Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, reviewed the dispute for WPTV and said the new information does not necessarily resolve the legal fight. Instead, he said questions could remain over what the city knew — or should have known — and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before the purchase. “You’re still going to have a dispute over whether the city knew or should have known that there were issues, and the city would argue from the developer standpoint, he should have done some due diligence,” Torcivia said. Shelli told WPTV that the city has not provided FDEP’s findings to him or his legal team. The lawsuit has potentially significant financial implications for Fort Pierce taxpayers. In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli. During a public meeting , the city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney’s fees and other expenses under Florida’s proposal-for-settlement rules. Commissioners took no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected. “Maybe it’s in everybody’s best interests if they go to mediation,” Torcivia said. WPTV reached out to the city for answers about its contamination claims and the status of the litigation. A spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation. For Mike Jenkins, the dispute has consequences beyond the courtroom. Jenkins and his family own the property beneath 12A Buoy, a restaurant at Fisherman’s Wharf. He said his family has owned the property for roughly 50 years. Jenkins said he was shocked when WFLX told him last year that contamination had become part of the city’s legal argument. “This place was clean,” Jenkins said, adding that environmental testing had been conducted in the area decades ago. He worries that simply associating Fisherman’s Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners. “You throw a word out like that — contaminated — that’s going to scare everybody, scare all the landowners,” Jenkins said. “I shouldn’t have been in this situation.” Shelli’s lawsuit against Fort Pierce remains pending as the city also navigates turnover within its legal department. And while FDEP’s testing did identify arsenic contamination in the broader area — including two exceedances on the city-owned property sold to Shelli — Beckler said the results he reviewed do not lead him to believe Fisherman’s Wharf is unsafe for recreational use. For now, the testing answers one question that has hung over Fisherman’s Wharf for more than a year: what is actually in the soil. What it means for the multimillion-dollar legal battle over the waterfront — however — remains unresolved. High surf and dangerous rip currents are posing a risk along Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast beaches heading into the weekend. A high risk of rip currents is in effect along the coast, along with a high surf advisory and small craft advisory. For coastal Palm Beach County, the National Weather Service says large breaking waves of 6 to 8 feet are expected in the surf zone. The high surf advisory remains in effect until 8 a.m. Saturday, while the high rip current risk continues through Saturday evening. A coastal flood statement is also in effect through Saturday evening, with isolated minor coastal flooding possible. Some water could reach low-lying roads and properties, and localized beach erosion is possible. See also: Former Palm Beach County Fire Rescue captain sentenced to 10 years in child porn case The National Weather Service warns that swimming and surfing conditions could be dangerous, with rip currents capable of sweeping even strong swimmers away from shore and into deeper water. The rough conditions have prompted several closures and warnings across the area. Local impacts In Lake Worth Beach, high waves prompted the closure of the Lake Worth Beach Pier. The city said on Instagram that the pier would close Friday, Sept. 25, because of wave conditions and is expected to reopen Sept. The beach and other businesses will remain open. In Delray Beach, medium-hazard yellow flags are expected because of heavy surf. The marina at the Boynton Beach Inlet is also closed until further notice. As of Friday, Boca Raton beaches are under red-flag conditions, according to the city's Recreation Services Department. The city said conditions for swimming and snorkeling are poor, and snorkeling is currently prohibited. Beachgoers should use caution throughout the weekend and pay attention to posted warning flags and lifeguard instructions.

Parking in Vero Beach is free, but overstaying your welcome is about to cost significantly more. Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to double most parking fines starting Oct. Fines for timed parking violations will increase from $20 to $40, while other miscellaneous infractions will rise from $30 to $60. Handicap violations will remain the same at $200 per violation. The city said the increases are the first since 2011. Vero Beach police sent a letter to the City Council in August requesting the rate increase, saying it would “encourage motorists to abide by the regulations.” Lt. Brian Kerensky said the goal is to keep parking spaces moving and bring more foot traffic to the city. “We have to kind of sometimes give them an incentive to move,” Kerensky said. “It creates turnover and can benefit from that.” For residents like Wendy Gage, who regularly parks along Beachland Boulevard, the change hits close to home. “The free parking is great...when it’s free,” Gage said. “We’ve been tagged multiple times for not moving it after two hours.” Neighbor Corey Wapnick said the increase is not fair because there are not enough spaces available to move to. “There’s only so much parking, and it’s usually on a beach day here, it’s very [full] there’s enough cars here that it’s almost impossible,” Wapnick said. Eugene Billero, who parks outside his real estate office, said a permit system could offer a better long-term solution for business owners and employees who need to park close to work. “You could do a permit for the month and charge X amount of dollars, and they’re going to get their money anyway,” Billero said. With property taxes on the ballot this November, Mayor John Cotugno said the timing of the fine increase was deliberate. “I think we did it at the opportune time,” Cotugno said. “Some of those courtesies that you paid, especially from a fee standpoint, we had to readdress.” Cotugno left the door open to exploring permit options and other long-term parking solutions. “I think that’s something that possibly should come up for discussion,” Cotugno said. The new fines take effect Oct.

A presentation at Stuart City Hall this week highlighted concerns about the potential impact of Amendment 3 on funding for waterway protection projects in Florida. The Rivers Coalition, which works to protect the health of the St. Lucie Estuary and Indian River Lagoon, heard from environmental policy adviser Eric Draper about how reduced property tax revenue could affect water management districts responsible for water supply, flood control and water quality. Mark Perry, president of the Rivers Coalition, said the amendment could lead to reduced services funded by property taxes. "What you have to do is evaluate. I'm going to get, reduce my tax liability over the next few years with this amendment. But is that worth the services that are going to be reduced?" Perry said. During the meeting, data showed that the South Florida Water Management District could lose approximately $98 million in annual revenue by 2030 if Amendment 3 passes. Martin County Commissioner Sarah Heard expressed concern about the potential impact on water quality projects. "The projects that improve water quality, that improve stormwater treatment, will be impacted, will be defunded," Heard said. Perry explained that local projects funded by property tax revenue, such as retention areas and large stormwater treatment systems, play a vital role in improving water quality by removing elements like nitrogen and phosphorus, which can prevent algae blooms. He said the passage of Amendment 3 would force local governments to decide whether to cut back on these projects or find alternative funding sources. "We're going to have a growing state and growing community here with growing runoff. That is going to happen," Perry said. A board member from the South Florida Water Management District told the Rivers Coalition that if Amendment 3 passes, it would affect the next fiscal year's budget, not the current one. However, they could not specify which projects might be impacted at this time. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments . Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Palm Beach County Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds , repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens; expand sports complexes; improve beach access and trail connections; and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District. The money would be used to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities. The bonds would be repaid through property taxes within the library district over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County’s existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending. Martin County Martin County’s local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. See also: Dead rodent in kitchen, 260 droppings & no hand-washing: 7 South Florida restaurants shut Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee . The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents’ preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy. Indian River and Okeechobee counties No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River or Okeechobee counties. Voters there will still decide statewide constitutional amendments and candidate races, but there are no known local bonds, referendums or advisory questions to add to the local ballot-issues list.

Florida cities and counties could begin billing residents separately for individual services if Amendment 3 passes — a change one expert compares to the difference between buying a ticket on United Airlines versus Spirit Airlines.We are hearing from all of you about Amendment 3, from comments to questions.WATCH BELOW: Amendment 3 could reshape how you pay for local servicesOne email I received this week was about all the separate entities on the property tax bill, such as the South Florida Water Management District. Leaders in cities and counties have been discussing all summer the impact of Amendment 3 and how to adjust to finding new funding. The email from Stephanie wondered, "Are those gonna be separate entities that send each homeowner a bill?" I recently talked with former Florida State Sen. "I think what most cities and counties will do is turn their sheriffs and fire departments into non-ad valorem taxes and create districts around those and individuals will see that as a separate line item on their tax bill," Brandes told me over the summer. "It's a little like buying a ticket on United and buying a ticket from Spirit Airlines," Brandes said. "Things are bundled up on a United ticket; they’re all broken out in the Spirit ticket, every service separately. I think That's where we’re headed here. We're headed to the Spirit Airlines of the Florida tax bill." Spirit Airlines, of course, no longer exists, but I think we all get the point. I'll keep looking for your comments and emails, and don't forget our Amendment 3 Town Hall on Oct.

Three Okeechobee men allegedly drove to Vero Beach before sunrise Thursday, crawled into the woods along I-95, and illegally harvested 350 pounds of palmetto berries, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office . At approximately 9:30 a.m. on Thursday, a corporal spotted a red vehicle parked in the woods along the state-owned median of I-95 near Mile Marker 159 in Vero Beach. Upon investigation, officers found Williams in the woods holding a white bag and plant pruners, actively cutting a stalk of berries from a saw palmetto tree. Williams was taken into custody after admitting he was harvesting the berries and revealing two other men were with him. A Fellsmere Police Department officer located Gabbard just south of Williams' location. See also: 2 killed, 2 critically hurt in head-on crash on Old Boynton Road Gabbard admitted that he and the others drove from Okeechobee before sunrise in his sister's car to harvest the berries. A search then began for the third suspect, identified only as "Ray". Deputies initially deployed a drone, but technical issues forced it down. Law enforcement issued loud verbal warnings before bringing in a Florida Highway Patrol K9 unit. The K9 tracked Howard to a thick canopy of razor-sharp saw palmetto trees. Howard refused commands to come out with his hands up and was ultimately apprehended by the K9. Howard later claimed he was napping and did not hear officers yelling, though deputies noted the sharp, serrated limbs and rough ground made his claim highly unlikely. All three men admitted post-Miranda that they did not have permission to be on state land nor did they hold required harvesting permits from the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS). Throughout the wooded median, authorities recovered multiple large bags filled with freshly cut saw palmetto berries weighing approximately 350 pounds total. All three suspects are being held without bond.

You can run, but according to Port St. Lucie police , you cannot hide especially under a hotel bed. Police said officers went to a hotel on Village Parkway on Tuesday after receiving information that 41-year-old Kenneth Robert Ferow II, who was wanted on a Martin County simple battery warrant, was inside a room. Ferow’s wife told officers he was not there, police said. But officers said they had credible information he was inside and continued investigating before getting permission to check the room. That's when officers looked beneath one of the beds and found Ferow hiding there, police said. Officers ordered Ferow to come out with his hands visible, and he was taken into custody without incident. Police said officers found a substance on Ferow that field-tested positive for methamphetamine . Two children, ages 14 and 8, were also inside the hotel room. See also: Deputies: Woman with pipe bomb in stolen car hits school bus while fleeing traffic stop Ferow was arrested on charges of possession of a controlled substance and two counts of child neglect, in addition to the outstanding warrant, police said.

A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County.The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95.WATCH BELOW: Shannon Marie Dillon makes her first appearanceAt around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard.Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118.During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia.Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. Anastasia Catholic School in Fort Pierce officially launched the Morning Star program on Thursday morning with a ribbon-cutting ceremony, marking the first program of its kind in the Diocese of Palm Beach to provide a full Catholic education experience for children with special needs. The program is called Morning Star, and officials with the diocese said it began as a pilot in August with seven students. Loved ones are grieving the loss of two young brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. The boys, 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark, grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt told WPBF 25 News that both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother also told WPBF 25 News they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the brothers' deaths. "Two children should still be alive today," Padrick said during a news conference. According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys told WPBF 25 News that the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident. Police said both survived and received treatment for their injuries. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday. "No family should have to endure the senseless loss of children," DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said. As the investigation continues in Georgia, the boys' family and members of the Fort Pierce community are focused on bringing them home to be laid to rest. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida. A presentation at Stuart City Hall this week highlighted concerns about the potential impact of Amendment 3 on funding for waterway protection projects in Florida. The Rivers Coalition, which works to protect the health of the St. Lucie Estuary and Indian River Lagoon, heard from environmental policy adviser Eric Draper about how reduced property tax revenue could affect water management districts responsible for water supply, flood control and water quality. Mark Perry, president of the Rivers Coalition, said the amendment could lead to reduced services funded by property taxes. "What you have to do is evaluate. I'm going to get, reduce my tax liability over the next few years with this amendment. But is that worth the services that are going to be reduced?" Perry said. During the meeting, data showed that the South Florida Water Management District could lose approximately $98 million in annual revenue by 2030 if Amendment 3 passes. Martin County Commissioner Sarah Heard expressed concern about the potential impact on water quality projects. "The projects that improve water quality, that improve stormwater treatment, will be impacted, will be defunded," Heard said. Perry explained that local projects funded by property tax revenue, such as retention areas and large stormwater treatment systems, play a vital role in improving water quality by removing elements like nitrogen and phosphorus, which can prevent algae blooms. He said the passage of Amendment 3 would force local governments to decide whether to cut back on these projects or find alternative funding sources. "We're going to have a growing state and growing community here with growing runoff. That is going to happen," Perry said. A board member from the South Florida Water Management District told the Rivers Coalition that if Amendment 3 passes, it would affect the next fiscal year's budget, not the current one. However, they could not specify which projects might be impacted at this time. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

A year after WFLX first investigated a contentious legal battle over the future of Fisherman’s Wharf, newly released environmental testing is raising fresh questions about a key argument in the dispute: contamination. The city of Fort Pierce previously told developer Chris Shelli that the waterfront property at the center of his lawsuit was “likely contaminated” and suggested the cost of remediation could essentially eliminate his claim for damages. But the city made that assertion before the Florida Department of Environmental Protection had completed its testing. According to site assessments obtained by WFLX, FDEP found arsenic above state residential cleanup targets in two soil samples on city-owned land sold to Shelli. However, both samples were less than twice the residential cleanup target, and an environmental researcher who reviewed the findings for WFLX said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming. “I don’t think it’s necessarily something to be too concerned with,” said Jordon Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute. Shelli purchased approximately 3.2 acres around Fisherman’s Wharf with plans to transform the waterfront into a new destination. But WFLX Investigates previously uncovered a significant complication with the deal. Roughly half of the property was subject to a state right-of-reverter restriction, meaning the land could revert to the state if it were sold for private development. Emails obtained by WFLX in our first investigation showed Fort Pierce commissioners did not learn until 2023 — about two years after the sale — that removing the restriction could cost nearly $2 million. Shelli ultimately sued the city for breach of contract. In 2025, an attorney for the city sent Shelli a letter arguing the property was “likely contaminated” and that the cost of “remediation” essentially “eliminates” his damages claim. At the time, however, FDEP’s environmental investigation was still underway. The environmental concerns extend beyond the Fisherman’s Wharf property itself. Land immediately north of Fisherman’s Wharf was once home to a citrus packing house. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site — a designation used for property where redevelopment may be complicated by actual or perceived environmental contamination. FDEP’s site assessment found several soil samples at the former citrus packing house contained arsenic above Florida’s residential and industrial cleanup targets. Beckler said those findings were consistent with the property’s historical industrial use. “Personally, there’s not really much in the report that alarmed me,” Beckler said. “I think the findings are consistent with the past industrial uses of the site.” One sample, however, stood out. FDEP found an arsenic concentration roughly 148 times Florida’s residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of the former citrus packing house property. But that hot spot was not on the land sold to Shelli. Shelli’s proposed development property sits across the street. FDEP did send letters to seven surrounding property owners warning about possible off-site contamination. One of those letters went to the city of Fort Pierce and identified arsenic above the residential cleanup target in two soil samples on city-owned property sold to Shelli. Those exceedances, however, were far smaller than the hot spot found at the former packing house. Both were less than twice the residential cleanup target. Beckler also noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and that naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils. “The vast majority of those samples, while, yes, they were above that residential standard, they weren’t that high above it,” Beckler said. The distinction could become important in Shelli’s lawsuit. FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels included in its assessment, but those parcels are associated with the former citrus packing house property. The agency did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli. That is notable because the city’s earlier letter specifically cited “remediation” when arguing that contamination would essentially eliminate Shelli’s damages. Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, reviewed the dispute for WPTV and said the new information does not necessarily resolve the legal fight. Instead, he said questions could remain over what the city knew — or should have known — and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before the purchase. “You’re still going to have a dispute over whether the city knew or should have known that there were issues, and the city would argue from the developer standpoint, he should have done some due diligence,” Torcivia said. Shelli told WPTV that the city has not provided FDEP’s findings to him or his legal team. The lawsuit has potentially significant financial implications for Fort Pierce taxpayers. In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli. During a public meeting , the city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney’s fees and other expenses under Florida’s proposal-for-settlement rules. Commissioners took no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected. “Maybe it’s in everybody’s best interests if they go to mediation,” Torcivia said. WPTV reached out to the city for answers about its contamination claims and the status of the litigation. A spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation. For Mike Jenkins, the dispute has consequences beyond the courtroom. Jenkins and his family own the property beneath 12A Buoy, a restaurant at Fisherman’s Wharf. He said his family has owned the property for roughly 50 years. Jenkins said he was shocked when WFLX told him last year that contamination had become part of the city’s legal argument. “This place was clean,” Jenkins said, adding that environmental testing had been conducted in the area decades ago. He worries that simply associating Fisherman’s Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners. “You throw a word out like that — contaminated — that’s going to scare everybody, scare all the landowners,” Jenkins said. “I shouldn’t have been in this situation.” Shelli’s lawsuit against Fort Pierce remains pending as the city also navigates turnover within its legal department. And while FDEP’s testing did identify arsenic contamination in the broader area — including two exceedances on the city-owned property sold to Shelli — Beckler said the results he reviewed do not lead him to believe Fisherman’s Wharf is unsafe for recreational use. For now, the testing answers one question that has hung over Fisherman’s Wharf for more than a year: what is actually in the soil. What it means for the multimillion-dollar legal battle over the waterfront — however — remains unresolved. With just six weeks until Florida voters choose their next governor, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds brought his campaign to Martin County on Wednesday for a roundtable discussion focused on affordability and other issues facing residents. For about an hour inside a small meeting room at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart, Rep. Donalds took questions from about a dozen Martin county voters, including insurance agents, realtors and homeowners. Rather than deliver a formal speech, Donalds encouraged an open discussion with community members. "Let's go around, introduce yourself and let's just have a dialogue," Donalds said at the start of the event. Questions centered largely on the rising cost of living, including homeowners insurance and healthcare costs. One homeowner asked Donalds what could be done about rising insurance costs. "What about homeowner's insurance because it's literally pricing people out of staying in their homes," the woman said. See also: Brightline may file Chapter 11 bankruptcy as soon as this week, reports say Donalds said higher construction costs have played a role in rising insurance premiums and outlined proposals he says would help lower costs for Floridians. The congressman also discussed his support for reducing property insurance premiums by 20% to 25% and his long-term goal of eliminating homestead property taxes. When another attendee raised concerns about increasing application fees and other costs imposed by local governments, Donalds said local officials should review their budgets and identify areas where spending can be cut. Throughout the discussion, Donalds emphasized making Florida more affordable for families, highlighting issues including insurance, housing and healthcare. "In healthcare, it's making sure we deal with stuff like dealing with in-network, out-of-network, prior authorizations," Donalds said. In an exclusive one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, Donalds was also asked about recent changes to his campaign website that removed prominent references to President Donald Trump's endorsement. "We're not distancing ourselves from President Trump," Donalds said. "We've been planning on making website changes for about two months now coming out of the primary. We wanted the website to be purely on the issues that we're campaigning on." Donalds added that he remains grateful for Trump's endorsement. Ron DeSantis has also endorsed Donalds in the race for governor. Donalds will face Democrat David Jolly in the November general election. Senior Advisor for the Jolly-Graham campaign Mark Riddle sent a statement saying: Byron Donalds is panicked about David Jolly's momentum and is trying to fool Florida voters with a desperate website change, but the reality is that Byron Donalds is nothing more than Trump's yes man," Riddle said. "He and Byron are tied at the hip for an agenda that has sent costs soaring. Florida voters are angry and ready for change, and David Jolly is ready to deliver. Donalds' stop in Martin County came after he appeared at an economic summit in Fort Lauderdale earlier in the day. Donalds and Democrat David Jolly spoke separately at the event, laying out different approaches to issues including property taxes and Florida's insurance market.

You can run, but according to Port St. Lucie police , you cannot hide especially under a hotel bed. He turned to Facebook for help."I made a Facebook post saying, hey, I don't know who needs to hear this, but this is ridiculous. Not to compare us to other schools, but they get a lot of stuff and we can't even," Weatherly said.Shark alum Bryan Rhoades saw the post and took action, sharing his own video online asking the community to step up."I need five business owners or people, whoever, to match my $1,000. We can get this done," Rhoades said.Rhoades owns Airbnbs in the area along with River Ride Cart Rentals LLC. He offered to donate $1,000 and encouraged other businesses to do the same. The response was swift."Within like an hour I had $2,000 and within I think three more days we had $10,350," Rhoades said.The old play clocks were stationary and had suffered significant wear and tear over the years, requiring repeated electrical repairs and parts replacements. The new clocks are a much-needed and quality upgrade."They're lit up, they're bright and they're bigger than I thought, they're great. They roll around so they can keep them out of the weather. It's going to be great for the team," Rhoades said.For Weatherly, the community response meant more than just new equipment."For the longest time, it seemed like we were just getting pushed to the side. And to see that there's people out there that still care and want to support and want to help, you know, it was great. It was amazing," Weatherly said.Rhoades said the outpouring support reflected the character of the Sebastian community."They just want to get out there and help. That's what it comes down to really. You know what I mean, the kids," Rhoades said.Reminding everyone, a small act of kindness, or in this case Facebook post, can generate solutions to fix an old, costly problem."Everybody is out there still trying to help each other, still willing to give and be part of the community and make things better for the kids," Weatherly said.The new play clocks are expected to debut at Sebastian River's next home football game on Oct.

Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments . Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Palm Beach County Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds , repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens; expand sports complexes; improve beach access and trail connections; and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District. The money would be used to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities. The bonds would be repaid through property taxes within the library district over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County’s existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending. Martin County Martin County’s local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. See also: Dead rodent in kitchen, 260 droppings & no hand-washing: 7 South Florida restaurants shut Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee . The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents’ preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy. Indian River and Okeechobee counties No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River or Okeechobee counties. Voters there will still decide statewide constitutional amendments and candidate races, but there are no known local bonds, referendums or advisory questions to add to the local ballot-issues list.

With just six weeks until Florida voters choose their next governor, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds brought his campaign to Martin County on Wednesday for a roundtable discussion focused on affordability and other issues facing residents. For about an hour inside a small meeting room at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart, Rep. Donalds took questions from about a dozen Martin county voters, including insurance agents, realtors and homeowners. Rather than deliver a formal speech, Donalds encouraged an open discussion with community members. "Let's go around, introduce yourself and let's just have a dialogue," Donalds said at the start of the event. Questions centered largely on the rising cost of living, including homeowners insurance and healthcare costs. One homeowner asked Donalds what could be done about rising insurance costs. "What about homeowner's insurance because it's literally pricing people out of staying in their homes," the woman said. See also: Brightline may file Chapter 11 bankruptcy as soon as this week, reports say Donalds said higher construction costs have played a role in rising insurance premiums and outlined proposals he says would help lower costs for Floridians. The congressman also discussed his support for reducing property insurance premiums by 20% to 25% and his long-term goal of eliminating homestead property taxes. When another attendee raised concerns about increasing application fees and other costs imposed by local governments, Donalds said local officials should review their budgets and identify areas where spending can be cut. Throughout the discussion, Donalds emphasized making Florida more affordable for families, highlighting issues including insurance, housing and healthcare. "In healthcare, it's making sure we deal with stuff like dealing with in-network, out-of-network, prior authorizations," Donalds said. In an exclusive one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, Donalds was also asked about recent changes to his campaign website that removed prominent references to President Donald Trump's endorsement. "We're not distancing ourselves from President Trump," Donalds said. "We've been planning on making website changes for about two months now coming out of the primary. We wanted the website to be purely on the issues that we're campaigning on." Donalds added that he remains grateful for Trump's endorsement. Ron DeSantis has also endorsed Donalds in the race for governor. Donalds will face Democrat David Jolly in the November general election. Senior Advisor for the Jolly-Graham campaign Mark Riddle sent a statement saying: Byron Donalds is panicked about David Jolly's momentum and is trying to fool Florida voters with a desperate website change, but the reality is that Byron Donalds is nothing more than Trump's yes man," Riddle said. "He and Byron are tied at the hip for an agenda that has sent costs soaring. Florida voters are angry and ready for change, and David Jolly is ready to deliver. Donalds' stop in Martin County came after he appeared at an economic summit in Fort Lauderdale earlier in the day. Donalds and Democrat David Jolly spoke separately at the event, laying out different approaches to issues including property taxes and Florida's insurance market.

You can run, but according to Port St. Lucie police , you cannot hide especially under a hotel bed. Police said officers went to a hotel on Village Parkway on Tuesday after receiving information that 41-year-old Kenneth Robert Ferow II, who was wanted on a Martin County simple battery warrant, was inside a room. Ferow’s wife told officers he was not there, police said. But officers said they had credible information he was inside and continued investigating before getting permission to check the room. That's when officers looked beneath one of the beds and found Ferow hiding there, police said. Officers ordered Ferow to come out with his hands visible, and he was taken into custody without incident. Police said officers found a substance on Ferow that field-tested positive for methamphetamine . Two children, ages 14 and 8, were also inside the hotel room. See also: Deputies: Woman with pipe bomb in stolen car hits school bus while fleeing traffic stop Ferow was arrested on charges of possession of a controlled substance and two counts of child neglect, in addition to the outstanding warrant, police said.

Loved ones are grieving the loss of two young brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. The boys, 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark, grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt told WPBF 25 News that both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother also told WPBF 25 News they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the brothers' deaths. "Two children should still be alive today," Padrick said during a news conference. According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys told WPBF 25 News that the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident. Police said both survived and received treatment for their injuries. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday. "No family should have to endure the senseless loss of children," DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said. As the investigation continues in Georgia, the boys' family and members of the Fort Pierce community are focused on bringing them home to be laid to rest. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida. Students returned to class as usual Wednesday after a 15-year-old Martin County High School student was accused of making a false bomb threat Tuesday, marking the fourth threat tied to the Stuart school in just over a week as parents voice growing concern. Families express concern after repeated threats: The repeated threats are taking a toll on some students and parents. CBS12 News spoke with freshman Maya and her mother, Liz, during school drop-off Wednesday morning. Maya described the response to one of the previous threats as frightening. The last bomb threat, it was crazy because, like a cop in Building Two, the alarm didn’t even go off, Maya said. A police officer had to go door to door and come get us and tell us to get out of the building. So, it was kind of like scary. Her mother said the string of threats has left her questioning what could happen each time she drops her daughter off at school. It is very concerning, Liz said. Every morning it’s like, should I bring her to school today? Is it going to be another one? Is this going to be the real one? District officials told CBS12 News counselors are readily available to support students if they are nervous from the ongoing issue. Student arrested in latest threat: The latest threat was reported Tuesday morning. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said 15-year-old sophomore Noah Taylor used FortifyFL, Florida’s school safety reporting system, to submit a report claiming bombs were inside a boys bathroom and would go off during third period. The school resource deputy determined the threat was not credible. Investigators said surveillance video and interviews with students led them to Taylor. Deputies said Taylor later admitted making the false report because Taylor wanted to get out of his third-period class. Taylor was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. Sheriff John Budensiek said Taylor is not believed to be connected to the three previous threats involving Martin County High School. Three earlier threats still under investigation: The Sheriff’s Office continues to investigate the other three threats. Budensiek said investigators traced the first threat to someone in Russia. The other two investigations remain active. The sheriff has warned students that false threats can carry serious and lasting consequences, including criminal charges and possible school discipline. For families such as Maya and Liz, the concern now is whether the threats will stop. The advice I give to my daughter is to stay calm. She’s very smart and quick to think, and I tell her to do what God is telling her right away. Follow the rules and what the teachers tell you, but you have to react how you feel in that moment. I know they’re not allowed to use their phones, but I really don’t care if you need to make a phone call in an emergency, just do it," said Liz. Maya said what initially felt unusual has started to feel more routine after so many incidents. A lot of people were screaming and calling their parents. Then, when they got home, they were looking on Facebook because Facebook has everything. We all talked about it and who we think is doing it. Everyone was saying it was Russia or something, but I don’t know," said Maya. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office continues working to determine who is responsible for the three unresolved threats. Martin County High School released the following statement: The safety and security of our students and staff remains our top priority. We appreciate the swift response and coordination of the Martin County Sheriff's Office, our School Resource Officers, and the District's Safety and Security Team, whose efforts allowed yesterday's false FortifyFL report involving Martin County High School to be quickly investigated, determined to be unfounded, and ultimately resolved with an arrest. Because the report was confirmed to be false, there is no additional law enforcement presence on campus related to this incident. Our two School Resource Officers remain on campus, and additional patrols continue as part of our normal daily safety operations. We also want to be clear: false threats and false reports are not pranks. They create fear, disrupt the educational environment, divert critical law enforcement resources, and carry serious disciplinary and criminal consequences. Individuals who make false reports should expect to be held fully accountable, exactly as how it unfolded yesterday. We understand these threats can cause fear and distress, and when we talk about student safety, we want them to feel safe as well. We will be providing additional services and staff during the school day, including School Social Service Workers and School Counselors, and we encourage students who need support to talk with them. We continue to encourage students, staff, and families to report legitimate safety concerns. Every report is taken seriously and investigated thoroughly because protecting our students and staff will always come first.

A Fort Lauderdale woman is facing multiple charges after authorities located a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County Tuesday night. According to the Broward Sheriff's Office, shortly after 9 p.m., Broward County Regional Communications received a report that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators, working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Deputies then spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. She was detained and identified as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale. Lucie police said officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. "The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. "PSLPD deployed both our K-9 unit and our drone resources." Drone video obtained by CBS12 News shows law enforcement officers from multiple agencies surrounding the stolen patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 before Dillon was arrested. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident. Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to investigators. The Broward County Sheriff's Office issued a statement crediting the coordination between agencies for bringing the incident to a safe end. The great coordination between all the agencies involved brought this incident to a peaceful conclusion. Nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty, and he reported his mark unit missing. The Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine exactly what happened and if any agency policy was violated. See also: Can Florida police pull you over for a license plate frame? What the new law says Investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and the Broward Sheriff's Office are still working the case.
