Palm Beach County commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on the construction of new hyperscale AI data centers Thursday, completing the final vote in a process that began this summer.WATCH BELOW: This is an issue WPTV has been following closely for several months. The moratorium adds a definition for a large-scale data center use to the Palm Beach County Unified Land Development Code and establishes a temporary halt on new facilities that meet that definition. The county's zoning commission recommended approval of the measure in August.The temporary ban gives county officials and staff time to research and draft comprehensive regulations for the fast-growing industry, which has faced increasing public scrutiny. A study from the University of Pennsylvania indicates that approximately 60% of Americans oppose data centers being built in their communities, a significant increase from earlier this year.The moratorium follows the commission's rejection of Project Tango, a controversial data center expansion proposal near the Arden community, back in July. Residents and commissioners cited concerns that the project could negatively affect nearby homes and Saddle View Elementary School.The county's action aligns with a national trend, as other local and state governments implement similar moratoriums to better understand and manage AI-related development.During a meeting earlier this year, commissioners and zoning staff discussed a range of potential rules that could be implemented following the one-year study period. Regulations under consideration include:Capping a facility's power consumption at 50 megawattsRequiring public disclosure of a data center's end-user or operatorEstablishing new restrictions on water use, noise levels and heat emissionsCreating a permanent task force to monitor the industry's evolutionPalm Beach County Commissioner Marci Woodward said she wants adequate time to hear from experts before the moratorium period ends."I want to hear from all the experts myself," Woodward said. "A year could fly by pretty quickly, and so I don't want to be at the end of this trying to cram it into another 12-hour meeting."Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores emphasized the importance of ongoing oversight."Whatever task force we put together should continue to study how this technology continues to evolve and what potential impacts it could play in the future," Flores said.With regard to data centers, the commission decided to look into hiring a consultant over establishing a committee. Either way, Woodward said the public needs to be involved."The public should come, listen, watch, show up, put in a card and speak every single time. I want to hear from them; we all want to hear from them, because this affects them just as much as it affects any of us," Woodward said. "A consultant or a committee, either way the public needs to participate in this."Palm Beach County Commissioner Gregg Weiss of District 2 said the vote reflects his responsibility to residents."It's in my responsibilities to look after the best interests of my fellow residents, and that means not just listening to their concerns but taking action," Weiss told WPTV's Joel Lopez. "And that is important when it comes to the health, safety of our community and when they're at risk," Weiss pointed to the rejected Project Tango proposal as a catalyst for the moratorium."Right here in Palm Beach County we recently had developers pushing for a hyper scale AI data center right next to a neighborhood and near an elementary school," he said. "Our community knew what happens when a data center comes to town, and we spoke up. Across the country, communities living near data centers have raised issues and concerns about water, electricity usage, wastewater discharges, and noise pollution."Weiss, a former technology executive who co-chaired a National Association of Counties committee on artificial intelligence in 2023, said he supports AI innovation but not at the expense of communities.WATCH PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW:"One of the reasons why I voted to deny this project is the sound impact study behind it. We're using the wrong metric, one that misses the low hum these facilities produce around the clock. That hum affects somebody's ability to get a good night's sleep or enjoy a quiet time out on their porch," Weiss said. "Palm Beach County has a message loud and clear, and that was hell no on AI data centers near our neighborhoods. I believe the promise of AI, but embracing innovation doesn't mean ignoring impact on our communities."Weiss also addressed the race for Florida governor and contrasting candidates' positions on data center development."Byron Donalds has earned the nickname 'Data Center Donalds,' and it fits. He's told Florida that pristine land is wide open to data centers, and he's told families to trust the process to find the truth about Byron Donalds. Data center developers have sent nearly a million dollars in campaign checks. When your community takes a backseat to donors bankrolling your campaign. You're not looking out for Palm Beach and you're not looking out for Florida," Weiss said. "Families here need a process they can trust. They need a governor who will pause it, study it, and get it right. Floridians across party lines are on the same page. No data centers in our neighborhoods. Byron Donalds wants to rush these projects forward. David Jolly wants answers first, and he's right. That's why I'm proud to stand with David Jolly, and come Nov. 3, I think the voters will do so too."Several residents who spoke during and after the meeting said the moratorium is only the beginning of a much longer discussion about how Palm Beach County should regulate data centers.Palm Beach County Democratic Environmental Caucus President Reinaldo Diaz said the moratorium is an opportunity to pause and assess the industry's impact."The people who want data centers now and right away are the people who are poised to benefit and profit off of them. Regardless of the cost of the community," Diaz told WPTV's Joel Lopez.He also raised concerns about the environmental impact of data centers on the Everglades ecosystem, particularly regarding water temperature."Palm Beach County is the main connection of sending clean water south to the southern Everglades," Diaz said. "The system starts from the Kissimmee River and goes into Lake Okeechobee, then we ideally want to send it south where the water is nice and clean for the rest of the Everglades, so that it makes its way into Florida Bay."He said the proposed Project Tango site was particularly problematic from an environmental standpoint."If you look at our map and if you were to choose the most egregious spot where you would propose something that generates this amount of heat, it would be where this project is being proposed," Diaz said. "That's at the critical juncture of the L8 Canal, the C-51, and the stormwater treatment areas. That's where that's the only connection if you think of it as pipes, that's the only pipe we have right now that sends water south to the lower Everglades." Diaz warned that even a small temperature increase from a data center could have significant consequences."This is a data center that will raise the temperature to the surrounding area by just a couple of degrees as soon as they turn it on. That's so critically important to the Everglades in the environment raising the temperature by just a couple degrees on water that is already stressed by heat raising temperature of the environment," he said. "You're raising the risk of things like cyanobacteria blooms, other bacteria blooms, poor water quality. That compromises all the effort that has been put into Everglades restoration."Palm Beach County conservation advocate Sergey Kelley, who addressed commissioners during public comment, called the unanimous vote a significant victory for residents who opposed Project Tango and pushed for stronger oversight of the industry. Kelley argued that public pressure helped change the county's approach and urged officials to use the next year to develop regulations that prioritize environmental protections and local concerns."I'm thankful to people speaking up and defending their backyards," Kelley said. "If we didn't speak out and got essentially very mad about it, they would have approved Project Tango and never approved a moratorium."Kelley said he remains concerned about the potential demands hyperscale data centers could place on water supplies, power infrastructure and environmentally sensitive lands, including wetlands and areas near the Everglades. He also argued that future projects should bear the full cost of any necessary infrastructure and environmental safeguards rather than shifting those expenses to taxpayers or utility customers. "It should not come from our taxes," Kelley said. "The cost should be totally to developers."He also argued the county's moratorium does not go as far as measures adopted elsewhere in Florida. He noted that Palm Beach County's pause applies to hyperscale data centers as defined by the state at 50 megawatts, while some municipalities have adopted lower thresholds. "At least six other municipalities have passed a 5- or 10-megawatt ban," Kelley said. He suggested county officials consider stricter limits or a longer moratorium as they spend the next year studying potential regulations, arguing that "50 megawatts still allows a lot of these big buildings."Meanwhile, Gary Brown, a member of the county's Planning Commission who said he was speaking as a resident, focused on the need for expertise and careful planning before any long-term regulations are adopted. Brown said rapidly evolving technology, environmental concerns and safety considerations make it critical for the county to gather reliable information before making permanent policy decisions."This stuff is moving at warp speed," Brown said. "The information you have today is old in a matter of minutes."Brown supported the commission's interest in hiring a consultant to help evaluate potential impacts and develop recommendations, saying local staff, subject-matter experts and residents should all have a role in the process. He said finding a consultant that have give commissioners the most accurate information would be worth the cost as they decide how and where and how data centers could operate in Palm Beach County."Give them the best data to make the best decisions that will protect us all," Brown said.While Brown said he left the meeting with "more questions" about how the county's review process will ultimately work, he cautioned against rushing decisions involving a technology that is changing rapidly. You can run, but according to Port St. Lucie police , you cannot hide especially under a hotel bed. Florida Democrats are turning concerns about data centers into a campaign message, calling for stronger safeguards and construction pauses as new polling shows most Florida adults oppose large facilities in their own communities.Republicans are emphasizing investment and community input as the debate over the buildings powering artificial intelligence expands from local meetings to the state's biggest campaigns.Watch more from Forrest Saunders on the reportDemocratic U.S. Senate nominee Angie Nixon brought that debate to Fort Meade this week, visiting a traditionally Republican area to hear residents' concerns."A lot of people are concerned with the environmental impacts and the health impacts of data centers coming into their neighborhoods," Nixon said.Nixon wants greater transparency around development decisions, stronger regulations and financial relief from developers if their projects hurt residents economically. She also raised concerns about potential increases in electricity and water bills.A new Stetson University survey found 54% of Florida adults oppose large data centers in their own communities, compared with 27% who support them.Democratic governor nominee David Jolly is making the issue part of his campaign, too.In a campaign video filmed in Northern Virginia, Jolly described concerns about pollution, noise and neighborhood disruption near existing facilities. He renewed his pledge to halt development temporarily in Florida."I’ve proposed a one-year moratorium," Jolly said. "My first day in office as governor, I will issue that moratorium."Democratic legislative candidates also are calling for a pause, tying the issue to their affordability agenda and residents’ ability to influence development decisions."They have broken trust with the voters," said Richard Lamondin, the Democratic nominee for Florida Senate District 38, referring to state leaders.Lamondin argued Tallahassee has weakened residents' ability to have a say in what gets built in their communities.Republican governor nominee Byron Donalds warned in an August interview that a statewide freeze could push investment elsewhere. He argued that attracting businesses and jobs is part of addressing affordability."But you can’t build for your life if you don’t have a high-paying job," Donalds said. "And you’re not going to have a high-paying job if you don’t have companies who invest in your state."Donalds supports protections for water supplies and utility customers, cooling systems that conserve water and keeping facilities away from homes.In the Senate race, Republican Sen. Ashley Moody has emphasized local and state decision-making."It needs to be up to the people of a community or a state to decide what works best for them," Moody said.The same Stetson survey shows both Republican nominees leading their Democratic opponents.Its likely-voter estimates, including undecided respondents who leaned toward a candidate, put Donalds at 51% to Jolly's 39%. Moody received 51% to Nixon's 40%.Those results do not establish how much data-center policy is influencing candidate preferences.Stetson surveyed 830 Florida adults through an online, nonprobability panel Sept. The university reported margins of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points for the adult results and 4.3 points for its estimates weighted for likely turnout.

The Okeechobee Musical & Arts Festival is once again going on hiatus, organizers announced via social media.The announcement comes after the festival returned in March from a two-year hiatus.In a Facebook post made Thursday afternoon, organizers said they have "faced some hard realities," and the festival industry is in a "difficult place" right now."With rising costs across talent, production and more ... it can be unforgiving, especially for independent promoters without the resources that large, multi-event companies have access to," the Facebook post said. A year after WPTV first investigated a contentious legal battle over the future of Fisherman's Wharf, newly released environmental testing is raising fresh questions about a key argument in the dispute: contamination.The city of Fort Pierce previously told developer Chris Shelli that the waterfront property at the center of his lawsuit was "likely contaminated" and suggested the cost of remediation could essentially eliminate his claim for damages.But the city made that assertion before the Florida Department of Environmental Protection had completed its testing.Those results are now in.According to site assessments obtained by WPTV, FDEP found arsenic above state residential cleanup targets in two soil samples on city-owned land sold to Shelli. However, both samples were less than twice the residential cleanup target, and an environmental researcher who reviewed the findings for WPTV said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming."I don't think it's necessarily something to be too concerned with," said Jordon Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.Shelli purchased approximately 3.2 acres around Fisherman’s Wharf with plans to transform the waterfront into a new destination.But WPTV Investigates previously uncovered a significant complication with the deal.Roughly half of the property was subject to a state right-of-reverter restriction, meaning the land could revert to the state if it were sold for private development.Emails obtained by WPTV in our first investigation showed Fort Pierce commissioners did not learn until 2023 — about two years after the sale — that removing the restriction could cost nearly $2 million.Shelli ultimately sued the city for breach of contract.In 2025, an attorney for the city sent Shelli a letter arguing the property was "likely contaminated" and that the cost of "remediation" essentially "eliminates" his damages claim.At the time, however, FDEP's environmental investigation was still underway.The environmental concerns extend beyond the Fisherman’s Wharf property itself.Land immediately north of Fisherman’s Wharf was once home to a citrus packing house. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site — a designation used for property where redevelopment may be complicated by actual or perceived environmental contamination.FDEP's site assessment found several soil samples at the former citrus packing house contained arsenic above Florida's residential and industrial cleanup targets.Beckler said those findings were consistent with the property's historical industrial use."Personally, there's not really much in the report that alarmed me," Beckler said. "I think the findings are consistent with the past industrial uses of the site."One sample, however, stood out.FDEP found an arsenic concentration roughly 148 times Florida's residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of the former citrus packing house property.But that hot spot was not on the land sold to Shelli.Shelli's proposed development property sits across the street.FDEP did send letters to seven surrounding property owners warning about possible off-site contamination. One of those letters went to the city of Fort Pierce and identified arsenic above the residential cleanup target in two soil samples on city-owned property sold to Shelli.Those exceedances, however, were far smaller than the hot spot found at the former packing house. Both were less than twice the residential cleanup target.Beckler also noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and that naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils."The vast majority of those samples, while, yes, they were above that residential standard, they weren't that high above it," Beckler said.The distinction could become important in Shelli's lawsuit.FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels included in its assessment, but those parcels are associated with the former citrus packing house property.The agency did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.That is notable because the city's earlier letter specifically cited "remediation" when arguing that contamination would essentially eliminate Shelli's damages.Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, reviewed the dispute for WPTV and said the new information does not necessarily resolve the legal fight.Instead, he said questions could remain over what the city knew — or should have known — and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before the purchase."You're still going to have a dispute over whether the city knew or should have known that there were issues, and the city would argue from the developer standpoint, he should have done some due diligence," Torcivia said.Shelli told WPTV that the city has not provided FDEP's findings to him or his legal team.The lawsuit has potentially significant financial implications for Fort Pierce taxpayers.In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli.During a public meeting, the city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules.Commissioners took no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected."Maybe it's in everybody's best interests if they go to mediation," Torcivia said.WPTV reached out to the city for answers about its contamination claims and the status of the litigation. A spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.For Mike Jenkins, the dispute has consequences beyond the courtroom.Jenkins and his family own the property beneath 12A Buoy, a restaurant at Fisherman's Wharf. He said his family has owned the property for roughly 50 years.Jenkins said he was shocked when WPTV told him last year that contamination had become part of the city's legal argument."This place was clean," Jenkins said, adding that environmental testing had been conducted in the area decades ago.He worries that simply associating Fisherman's Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners."You throw a word out like that — contaminated — that's going to scare everybody, scare all the landowners," Jenkins said. "I shouldn't have been in this situation."Shelli's lawsuit against Fort Pierce remains pending as the city also navigates turnover within its legal department.And while FDEP's testing did identify arsenic contamination in the broader area — including two exceedances on the city-owned property sold to Shelli — Beckler said the results he reviewed do not lead him to believe Fisherman’s Wharf is unsafe for recreational use.For now, the testing answers one question that has hung over Fisherman's Wharf for more than a year: what is actually in the soil.What it means for the multimillion-dollar legal battle over the waterfront — however — remains unresolved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Jupiter Island had Florida’s fastest-growing home prices over the past year, according to a new Stacker analysis of Zillow data, while Palm Beach County communities accounted for 15 of the 50 places ranked statewide. The typical Jupiter Island home was valued at about $10.14 million in August, an increase of nearly $1.16 million, or 12.9%, from a year earlier, the study found. The Martin County barrier-island town ranked No. The Stacker report examined the dollar change in Zillow’s Home Value Index for all homes during the 12 months ending in August 2026. The figures are estimates of a typical home’s value, not the median price paid in individual sales. Jupiter Island’s typical home value was the highest in the study outside of a handful of South Florida luxury enclaves. Still, its one-year dollar increase outpaced every other city and town in the ranking, including Golden Beach, Fisher Island and Lake Buena Vista. The gain adds to a longer run-up in values on Jupiter Island. Its typical home value has increased by about $2.89 million, or 39.9%, over the past five years, according to the analysis. Sewalls Point was the other Treasure Coast community included in the statewide rankings. 18, with a typical home value of about $1.41 million, up $52,523, or 3.9%, from last year. The Martin County community’s typical home value has risen about $360,627, or 34.5%, over five years. Palm Beach County’s coastal luxury market was especially prominent in the rankings. Manalapan ranked fifth statewide. The typical home there was valued at just under $3.8 million, after climbing about $302,817 in a year an 8.7% gain. Gulf Stream ranked sixth, where the typical home value reached about $2.76 million, up $244,531, or 9.7%. Golf, a small Palm Beach County community west of Delray Beach, ranked seventh. Its typical home value increased by about $240,496 over the year to roughly $3.1 million. Jupiter Inlet Colony , a small waterfront community near the Jupiter Inlet, ranked 10th. Its typical home value was about $3.86 million, up $113,350, or 3%, from a year earlier. The list also showed growth beyond the county’s wealthiest waterfront towns. Palm Beach Gardens , Boca Raton , Lake Park, Limestone Creek, Mangonia Park and Belle Glade all posted one-year increases in typical home values. See also: Brightline may file Chapter 11 bankruptcy as soon as this week, reports say Mangonia Park and Belle Glade had two of the strongest percentage gains among Palm Beach County communities included in the analysis, despite much lower typical home values than the county’s coastal enclaves. Mangonia Park’s typical home value rose 6.9% to about $293,410, while Belle Glade’s rose 6.4% to about $293,282. Palm Beach Shores also posted a 6.7% one-year increase, with a typical home value of about $865,332. Ocean Ridge saw a 4.9% increase to about $1.5 million, while Lake Clarke Shores rose 4.7% to about $668,485. Nationally, the typical home value was $369,678 in August, up 1.3% over the year, according to the report. Stacker said price growth has slowed in some places amid higher mortgage rates, though limited housing supply continues to push values higher in many markets. The local results underscore the wide range of housing costs across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast: In the same ranking, Jupiter Island’s estimated typical home value was more than 34 times higher than Belle Glade’s.

Ron DeSantis signed his 18th death warrant of the year Friday. William Reaves , convicted of the 1986 killing of an Indian River County Sheriff's deputy, is set to be executed by lethal injection at Florida State Prison in Stark on Oct. According to court records, Reaves shot Deputy Sheriff Richard Raczkowski four times in the back outside a Zippy Mart convenience store near Vero Beach on September 23, 1986. Reaves had called 911 from a pay phone because he didn’t have money for a cab. Raczkowski, who was dispatched to the call, called the 911 dispatcher to order a cab for Reaves and to inquire about outstanding warrants. During this time, Reaves said a gun fell out of his pants. After the deputy attempted to block Reaves from retrieving the gun, a struggle ensued and Reaves wrestled the weapon away from Raczkowski. The deputy asked Reaves not to kill him and turned to run away, at which time Reaves fired four times into Raczkowski’s back. He would die a short time later. Reaves went to the home of a friend, who later told police Reaves confessed to shooting the deputy as he was high on cocaine and panicked. Reaves was arrested three days later at a bus stop and charged with first-degree murder, possession of a firearm by a convicted felon and trafficking in cocaine. He entered a not guilty plea but was found guilty of first-degree murder in September 1987, with the jury giving a unanimous recommendation for the death penalty. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction and sentence in 1991, finding the trial court erred by allowing a prosecutor on the case who had previously defended Reaves in a criminal matter. A second jury again found Reaves guilty of first-degree murder in February 1992, with the jury voting 10-2 to recommend a death sentence. Florida leads the nation in executions, carrying out 15 of them this year after 19 were performed last year, the most in a single year by the state since the U.S. Supreme Court ended a four-year nationwide moratorium on capital punishment in 1976. Curtis Wilkie Beasley, 77, is scheduled for execution on Sept. 29 for the 1995 murder of a Polk County woman who was bludgeoned with a hammer in her home. Last Friday, DeSantis signed a warrant for William Lee Thompson, 74, to be executed Oct. 13 for the murder, kidnapping, and sexual battery of Sally Ivester more than 50 years ago in North Miami Beach. Counsel for Reaves quickly filed a motion Friday for a stay until pending motions for a stay they have also filed regarding Thompson are resolved. See also: Driver hits 120 mph on I-95 before crashing into tree, fence while fleeing FHP Both clients are due the best representation counsel can provide, particularly when both clients are facing a scheduled execution date, stated the motion from Reaves’ counsel Brittney Lacy. The state has conducted 43 executions under DeSantis, or 31 percent of the 140 carried out since 1976. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers has been pushing for DeSantis to sign the warrant for Reaves as he is one that, in my opinion, should be a priority case. "It's very frustrating as the Sheriff, Flowers told WPEC last July. We want people to know that we're holding people accountable. And in this case, yes, he's jailed, yes, he's sitting there, but ultimately it was decided a long time ago that he would face the death penalty, and it's time for him to actually face the consequences. He's exhausted all of his appeals. Many other cases just like his have resulted in execution, and for some reason, he continues to cost us taxpayer dollars every single day.

In preparation for a powerful nor’easter expected to hit New England this weekend, Major League Baseball moved what could be a pivotal game from Sunday to Friday in hopes of avoiding a rainout.MLB said Sunday’s game between the Chicago Cubs and Boston Red Sox will now be played Friday afternoon as part of a day-night doubleheader. A year after WPTV first investigated a contentious legal battle over the future of Fisherman's Wharf, newly released environmental testing is raising fresh questions about a key argument in the dispute: contamination.The city of Fort Pierce previously told developer Chris Shelli that the waterfront property at the center of his lawsuit was "likely contaminated" and suggested the cost of remediation could essentially eliminate his claim for damages.But the city made that assertion before the Florida Department of Environmental Protection had completed its testing.Those results are now in.According to site assessments obtained by WPTV, FDEP found arsenic above state residential cleanup targets in two soil samples on city-owned land sold to Shelli. However, both samples were less than twice the residential cleanup target, and an environmental researcher who reviewed the findings for WPTV said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming."I don't think it's necessarily something to be too concerned with," said Jordon Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.Shelli purchased approximately 3.2 acres around Fisherman’s Wharf with plans to transform the waterfront into a new destination.But WPTV Investigates previously uncovered a significant complication with the deal.Roughly half of the property was subject to a state right-of-reverter restriction, meaning the land could revert to the state if it were sold for private development.Emails obtained by WPTV in our first investigation showed Fort Pierce commissioners did not learn until 2023 — about two years after the sale — that removing the restriction could cost nearly $2 million.Shelli ultimately sued the city for breach of contract.In 2025, an attorney for the city sent Shelli a letter arguing the property was "likely contaminated" and that the cost of "remediation" essentially "eliminates" his damages claim.At the time, however, FDEP's environmental investigation was still underway.The environmental concerns extend beyond the Fisherman’s Wharf property itself.Land immediately north of Fisherman’s Wharf was once home to a citrus packing house. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site — a designation used for property where redevelopment may be complicated by actual or perceived environmental contamination.FDEP's site assessment found several soil samples at the former citrus packing house contained arsenic above Florida's residential and industrial cleanup targets.Beckler said those findings were consistent with the property's historical industrial use."Personally, there's not really much in the report that alarmed me," Beckler said. "I think the findings are consistent with the past industrial uses of the site."One sample, however, stood out.FDEP found an arsenic concentration roughly 148 times Florida's residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of the former citrus packing house property.But that hot spot was not on the land sold to Shelli.Shelli's proposed development property sits across the street.FDEP did send letters to seven surrounding property owners warning about possible off-site contamination. One of those letters went to the city of Fort Pierce and identified arsenic above the residential cleanup target in two soil samples on city-owned property sold to Shelli.Those exceedances, however, were far smaller than the hot spot found at the former packing house. Both were less than twice the residential cleanup target.Beckler also noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and that naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils."The vast majority of those samples, while, yes, they were above that residential standard, they weren't that high above it," Beckler said.The distinction could become important in Shelli's lawsuit.FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels included in its assessment, but those parcels are associated with the former citrus packing house property.The agency did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.That is notable because the city's earlier letter specifically cited "remediation" when arguing that contamination would essentially eliminate Shelli's damages.Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, reviewed the dispute for WPTV and said the new information does not necessarily resolve the legal fight.Instead, he said questions could remain over what the city knew — or should have known — and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before the purchase."You're still going to have a dispute over whether the city knew or should have known that there were issues, and the city would argue from the developer standpoint, he should have done some due diligence," Torcivia said.Shelli told WPTV that the city has not provided FDEP's findings to him or his legal team.The lawsuit has potentially significant financial implications for Fort Pierce taxpayers.In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli.During a public meeting, the city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules.Commissioners took no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected."Maybe it's in everybody's best interests if they go to mediation," Torcivia said.WPTV reached out to the city for answers about its contamination claims and the status of the litigation. A spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.For Mike Jenkins, the dispute has consequences beyond the courtroom.Jenkins and his family own the property beneath 12A Buoy, a restaurant at Fisherman's Wharf. He said his family has owned the property for roughly 50 years.Jenkins said he was shocked when WPTV told him last year that contamination had become part of the city's legal argument."This place was clean," Jenkins said, adding that environmental testing had been conducted in the area decades ago.He worries that simply associating Fisherman's Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners."You throw a word out like that — contaminated — that's going to scare everybody, scare all the landowners," Jenkins said. "I shouldn't have been in this situation."Shelli's lawsuit against Fort Pierce remains pending as the city also navigates turnover within its legal department.And while FDEP's testing did identify arsenic contamination in the broader area — including two exceedances on the city-owned property sold to Shelli — Beckler said the results he reviewed do not lead him to believe Fisherman’s Wharf is unsafe for recreational use.For now, the testing answers one question that has hung over Fisherman's Wharf for more than a year: what is actually in the soil.What it means for the multimillion-dollar legal battle over the waterfront — however — remains unresolved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Brightline is expected to file for bankruptcy as soon as this week, according to several financial media outlets, including Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.The rail line is planning an imminent Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing to restructure about $5.5 billion in debt, according to The Wall Street Journal.Despite the filing, Brightline plans to keep its trains running on schedule.The company reported in June that total ridership has continued to grow."For June 2026, total ridership was 292,339, up 15% year-over-year, with average daily ridership of 9,745," Brightline's June ridership report said.Brightline has been offering service from South Florida to Orlando for the past three years, a massive expansion project that cost the company $6 billion and took four years to complete.A proposed Brightline station in downtown Stuart has faced a winding road of funding discussions, local debates and regional planning. Brightline selected Stuart as its designated Treasure Coast stop more than two years ago, but project timelines and cost-sharing agreements have remained a frequent topic of debate.The company's June ridership report also mentioned that they still plan to construct a station in Cocoa and to extend the rail system from Orlando to Tampa.

The Okeechobee Musical & Arts Festival is once again going on hiatus, organizers announced via social media.The announcement comes after the festival returned in March from a two-year hiatus.In a Facebook post made Thursday afternoon, organizers said they have "faced some hard realities," and the festival industry is in a "difficult place" right now."With rising costs across talent, production and more ... it can be unforgiving, especially for independent promoters without the resources that large, multi-event companies have access to," the Facebook post said. Two high-profile animal hoarding cases in Martin County this summer — and a third in Palm Beach County — have prompted questions about whether more can be done to prevent animal neglect before it reaches a crisis point. The answers, experts say, are not simple.On July 20, Martin County deputies rescued more than 100 cats and dogs from a house near Hobe Sound."This is the worst animal hoarding case that I've seen," Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the scene.Exactly three weeks later, on Aug. 10, the same group of deputies rescued 36 border collies from a Palm City house piled with feces and rot. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, which was still handling rescue efforts of the previous case, then said this was the worst hoarding case they'd ever seen.On Sept. 16, Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputies, serving an unrelated arrest warrant near Lantana, rescued 13 dogs from another feces-filled home. According to the affidavit, seven of the dogs were confined inside 2 cages.Cesar Perea, vice president of the American Humane Society, said cases like these are not unusual."Unfortunately, it's really common throughout the country to see this level of neglect going on," Perea said.When asked why it is so common, Perea pointed to intent gone wrong."It's typically well-intentioned, whether it's a breeding operation or a rescue operation that just eventually just goes wrong," Perea said.The American Humane Society monitors cases like these across the U.S. and assists law enforcement and local animal rescues when called upon. Perea said he does not believe the number of cases is necessarily growing — but that public awareness is."I don't know if it's so much these cases are increasing. I think a lot of it has to do with awareness. I think with social media and people being involved, I think we're experiencing like a renaissance of people just not standing for it," Perea said.That shift in public attitude is reaching lawmakers, according to Kate MacFall, the Florida state director for Humane World for Animals. MacFall works in Tallahassee, where her job is to help shape Florida's animal welfare policy."Our legislators are filing more animal bills," MacFall said. "We've done a lot of really good things in recent years, but there's a lot of work to be done."But preventing hoarding cases specifically is more complicated."It's a bigger picture question," MacFall said.A major obstacle is the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures. Budensiek addressed the limitation when initially asked about the Border Collie case, after a neighbor raised concerns about the dogs at a WPTV Let's Hear It community meet-up."There's laws and case law that say you can go this far and you can go no further unless you have probable cause," Budensiek said.That constitutional boundary makes the problem difficult to address through legislation alone."A lot of times with legislation you create unintended consequences, so you have to be really careful," Perea said.For now, advocates say individual action remains the most effective tool."If you see something, say something. I mean, that's for a reason," MacFall said.Some policy efforts are in the works. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, has expressed interest in a mandatory breeder registry. In Palm Beach County, commissioners are expected to consider higher fees and mandatory inspections for hobby breeders later this fall.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Students returned to class as usual Wednesday after a 15-year-old Martin County High School student was accused of making a false bomb threat Tuesday, marking the fourth threat tied to the Stuart school in just over a week as parents voice growing concern. Families express concern after repeated threats: The repeated threats are taking a toll on some students and parents. CBS12 News spoke with freshman Maya and her mother, Liz, during school drop-off Wednesday morning. Maya described the response to one of the previous threats as frightening. The last bomb threat, it was crazy because, like a cop in Building Two, the alarm didn’t even go off, Maya said. A police officer had to go door to door and come get us and tell us to get out of the building. So, it was kind of like scary. Her mother said the string of threats has left her questioning what could happen each time she drops her daughter off at school. It is very concerning, Liz said. Every morning it’s like, should I bring her to school today? Is it going to be another one? Is this going to be the real one? District officials told CBS12 News counselors are readily available to support students if they are nervous from the ongoing issue. Student arrested in latest threat: The latest threat was reported Tuesday morning. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said 15-year-old sophomore Noah Taylor used FortifyFL, Florida’s school safety reporting system, to submit a report claiming bombs were inside a boys bathroom and would go off during third period. The school resource deputy determined the threat was not credible. Investigators said surveillance video and interviews with students led them to Taylor. Deputies said Taylor later admitted making the false report because Taylor wanted to get out of his third-period class. Taylor was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. Sheriff John Budensiek said Taylor is not believed to be connected to the three previous threats involving Martin County High School. Three earlier threats still under investigation: The Sheriff’s Office continues to investigate the other three threats. Budensiek said investigators traced the first threat to someone in Russia. The other two investigations remain active. The sheriff has warned students that false threats can carry serious and lasting consequences, including criminal charges and possible school discipline. For families such as Maya and Liz, the concern now is whether the threats will stop. The advice I give to my daughter is to stay calm. She’s very smart and quick to think, and I tell her to do what God is telling her right away. Follow the rules and what the teachers tell you, but you have to react how you feel in that moment. I know they’re not allowed to use their phones, but I really don’t care if you need to make a phone call in an emergency, just do it," said Liz. Maya said what initially felt unusual has started to feel more routine after so many incidents. A lot of people were screaming and calling their parents. Then, when they got home, they were looking on Facebook because Facebook has everything. We all talked about it and who we think is doing it. Everyone was saying it was Russia or something, but I don’t know," said Maya. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office continues working to determine who is responsible for the three unresolved threats. Martin County High School released the following statement: The safety and security of our students and staff remains our top priority. We appreciate the swift response and coordination of the Martin County Sheriff's Office, our School Resource Officers, and the District's Safety and Security Team, whose efforts allowed yesterday's false FortifyFL report involving Martin County High School to be quickly investigated, determined to be unfounded, and ultimately resolved with an arrest. Because the report was confirmed to be false, there is no additional law enforcement presence on campus related to this incident. Our two School Resource Officers remain on campus, and additional patrols continue as part of our normal daily safety operations. We also want to be clear: false threats and false reports are not pranks. They create fear, disrupt the educational environment, divert critical law enforcement resources, and carry serious disciplinary and criminal consequences. Individuals who make false reports should expect to be held fully accountable, exactly as how it unfolded yesterday. We understand these threats can cause fear and distress, and when we talk about student safety, we want them to feel safe as well. We will be providing additional services and staff during the school day, including School Social Service Workers and School Counselors, and we encourage students who need support to talk with them. We continue to encourage students, staff, and families to report legitimate safety concerns. Every report is taken seriously and investigated thoroughly because protecting our students and staff will always come first.

A Fort Lauderdale woman is facing multiple charges after authorities located a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County Tuesday night. According to the Broward Sheriff's Office, shortly after 9 p.m., Broward County Regional Communications received a report that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators, working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Deputies then spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. She was detained and identified as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale. Lucie police said officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. "The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. "PSLPD deployed both our K-9 unit and our drone resources." Drone video obtained by CBS12 News shows law enforcement officers from multiple agencies surrounding the stolen patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 before Dillon was arrested. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident. Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to investigators. The Broward County Sheriff's Office issued a statement crediting the coordination between agencies for bringing the incident to a safe end. The great coordination between all the agencies involved brought this incident to a peaceful conclusion. Nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty, and he reported his mark unit missing. The Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine exactly what happened and if any agency policy was violated. See also: Can Florida police pull you over for a license plate frame? What the new law says Investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and the Broward Sheriff's Office are still working the case.

By: Scott Sutton Posted and last updated MARTIN COUNTY, Fla. — A barn that caught fire in Martin County on Thursday caused large flames and sent black smoke into the air that could be seen for miles. A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff’s Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. A 37-year-old man is facing charges after police say he was the aggressor in a confrontation that ended with him being shot at a Port St. Lucie restaurant Saturday afternoon.Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. 19 when a 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. When the man left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside.Outside surveillance footage showed Harris pushing the man and advancing toward him while the victim backed away, according to police. Witnesses reported seeing Harris with a knife just before the shooting.The 25-year-old fired one round, striking Harris in the chest. Harris then went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders began providing aid and called 911.Officers responding to reports of gunfire found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris' waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris' front pocket, police said.The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm.Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. He will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital.No criminal charges are pending against the shooter at this time.

Some residents in Port St. Lucie and their homeowners' association are at odds over dead trees. People who live in Cadence at Tradition received a notice dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc., saying the dead tree or dead trees on their property need to be replaced. The notice says: "Your assistance and cooperation are requested regarding the following: Landscaping-Dead Tree- The deceased tree(s) on your property is in need of attention." Residents say the trees are on the swale, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and numerous trees were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the swale, some residents say it should be the HOA 's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners. "It's just a little bit frustrating and disappointing that we, as homeowners, have to endure this from the HOA," said Keyla Peguero, a homeowner at Cadence at Tradition. Recently the HOA has removed many of the dead trees, leaving holes in the ground where residents are supposed to put in new trees, at the homeowners' expense. But homeowners such as Chip Collison say the dead trees were in common areas, not their yards, so they want the HOA to pay for new trees in the swales. "You think the swale is a common area?" we asked Collison. "Based on the documentation I've read? The notice sent to homeowners goes on to say: "We kindly request you address this matter by 9/30/26 to avoid escalation." See also: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees. Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead. "We're well into hurricane season now. If we plant new trees, no one can predict the future. These trees could be freshly planted. We get a strong hurricane come through, they're all gone, and they're gonna have to be redone again," Collison said. Peguero says she replaced a dead tree in the swale in front of her house, at a total cost of $300 to remove the dead tree, haul it away and replace it with a new tree. She says she's not willing to do it again and shouldn't have had to do it in the first place. A public relations firm for The Cadence at Tradition HOA sent us this written statement: Currently, the HOA is replacing thousands of dead trees and shrubs in the common areas that have yet to recover from the last freeze. In the limited common areas, such as the rights of way immediately adjacent to and between individual lots, including areas containing sidewalks and driveway aprons, residents are responsible for replacing trees and maintaining these areas. Because the HOA is currently purchasing and installing trees in bulk, we’ve invited residents to participate in the program. This allows homeowners to share in the cost savings while ensuring that tree replacements around their homes are selected and installed professionally.

Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments . Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Palm Beach County Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds , repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens; expand sports complexes; improve beach access and trail connections; and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District. The money would be used to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities. The bonds would be repaid through property taxes within the library district over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County’s existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending. Martin County Martin County’s local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. See also: Dead rodent in kitchen, 260 droppings & no hand-washing: 7 South Florida restaurants shut Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee . The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents’ preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy. Indian River and Okeechobee counties No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River or Okeechobee counties. Voters there will still decide statewide constitutional amendments and candidate races, but there are no known local bonds, referendums or advisory questions to add to the local ballot-issues list.

Lucie road rage incident that escalated into a physical fight and shooting landed two men in handcuffs Thursday. Lucie Police Department, the incident happened at about 6:30 p.m. near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace. Police said that before the shooting, one driver believed he was being followed after merging onto Southwest Crosstown Parkway. The vehicles had passed each other, and one driver believed the other had cut him off. Investigators determined there was no intentional following, police said. One of the drivers, identified as Tylon Kukielka, 57, was driving with his girlfriend to her home after leaving a local restaurant. The other driver, identified as Dean Plotts, 41, was traveling in the same direction. Police said the situation escalated into a physical fight near Southwest Brevity Terrace, when Plotts got out of his truck and confronted Kukielka's car. "He got out of his vehicle and approached the other vehicle, which was parked in front of him, and he approached it, and he punched the driver of that vehicle through the open window," said Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk. See also: Formerly conjoined twins see each other face-to-face after historic separation surgery Investigators say Plotts went back to his own vehicle, but Kukielka followed with a gun and shot him multiple times. While an arrest report indicates the two men were facing each other when the shots were fired, Niemczyk said Plotts wasn't confronting Kukielka again he was trying to get away. "The reason they were facing the same direction is because he was turning to his open car door, [trying] to get back in his vehicle," Niemczyk said. "So he wasn't actually going back to confront [him]." A St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy traveling in the area witnessed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also taken to a hospital for a medical evaluation. Investigators recovered surveillance video and shell casings during the investigation. Detectives later charged Kukielka with attempted homicide. Plotts was charged with burglary with assault or battery a charge Niemczyk said surprises people unfamiliar with the statute. "Most people will associate that with a house or a business," Niemczyk said. "But you can also commit burglary of a conveyance, which is a vehicle. So by punching the individual, he broke the plane of that vehicle." The incident remains under investigation. Niemczyk said road rage incidents like this one have become more common in Port St. "I would say over the last few years, yeah, we've had quite a few road rage incidents in this city," Niemczyk said. "And obviously with the increased volume of traffic in the community and the congestion that a lot of our residents are accustomed to, frustration comes along with that."

Loved ones are grieving the loss of two young brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. The boys, 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark, grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt told WPBF 25 News that both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother also told WPBF 25 News they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the brothers' deaths. "Two children should still be alive today," Padrick said during a news conference. According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys told WPBF 25 News that the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident. Police said both survived and received treatment for their injuries. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday. "No family should have to endure the senseless loss of children," DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said. As the investigation continues in Georgia, the boys' family and members of the Fort Pierce community are focused on bringing them home to be laid to rest. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida. A confrontation between teenagers at an Indiantown school bus stop escalated into a man pulling a gun on two teens, according to a Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. Palm Beach County is changing course on how it will develop new regulations for AI data centers during its one-year moratorium, scrapping a planned resident-led task force and instead hiring outside consultants at a potential cost of up to $2 million to taxpayers.The decision marks a significant shift from the county's initial plan, which emphasized creating a resident task force to help guide the new rules. The pivot, made during Thursday's commission meeting, is drawing mixed reactions from residents who will ultimately foot the bill.Commissioners argued that the complexity of AI data center technology requires specialized knowledge that a volunteer committee may not possess."I don’t know that we need a committee, I think what we need is a consultant that’s an expert in the field," said Commissioner Joel Flores, who originally championed the task force idea.Commissioner Marci Woodward agreed, suggesting that hiring experts would be more efficient. "I fear we are adding an extra layer of work not only for the staff but also for interested parties and the public who want to participate in this as well," she said.However, the expertise comes with a hefty price tag. Early estimates presented at the meeting place the cost of hiring a consulting firm between $200,000 and $2 million.The decision to spend taxpayer money on outside experts rather than empower a resident committee is not sitting well with everyone."If it's going to cost taxpayer money, to me, it seems like it's a superfluous use of that money," said resident David Salvato.Taxpayer Juan Rivero expressed concern about losing direct public influence. "Who's paying for them?" he asked. "We don't have a voice on it, even though we're paying for it."Other residents, like Vivian Diaz, believe it's a necessary expense. "It's the best thing we can do as a community," she said. "Especially we paying for it."While the formal task force is off the table, residents can still voice their opinions during public comment periods at future commission meetings. For some, the core issue is ensuring the final regulations serve the community's best interests."It shouldn't be polarized. It's 'What's good for the community? What's the bottom line?'" Rivero said.
