Parking in Vero Beach is free, but overstaying your welcome is about to cost significantly more. Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to double most parking fines starting Oct. WATCH BELOW: Vero Beach doubling parking fines Fines for timed parking violations will increase from $20 to $40, while other miscellaneous infractions will rise from $30 to $60. Handicap violations will remain the same at $200 per violation. The city said the increases are the first since 2011. Vero Beach police sent a letter to the City Council in August requesting the rate increase, saying it would "encourage motorists to abide by the regulations." Lt. Brian Kerensky said the goal is to keep parking spaces moving and bring more foot traffic to the city. "We have to kind of sometimes give them an incentive to move," Kerensky said. "It creates turnover and can benefit from that." For residents like Wendy Gage, who regularly parks along Beachland Boulevard, the change hits close to home. "The free parking is great...when it's free," Gage said. "We've been tagged multiple times for not moving it after two hours." Neighbor Corey Wapnick said the increase is not fair because there are not enough spaces available to move to. "There's only so much parking, and it's usually on a beach day here, it's very [full] there's enough cars here that it's almost impossible," Wapnick said. Eugene Billero, who parks outside his real estate office, said a permit system could offer a better long-term solution for business owners and employees who need to park close to work. "You could do a permit for the month and charge X amount of dollars, and they're going to get their money anyway," Billero said. With property taxes on the ballot this November, Mayor John Cotugno said the timing of the fine increase was deliberate. "I think we did it at the opportune time," Cotugno said. "Some of those courtesies that you paid, especially from a fee standpoint, we had to readdress." Cotugno left the door open to exploring permit options and other long-term parking solutions. "I think that's something that possibly should come up for discussion," Cotugno said. The new fines take effect Oct.

Shark pride runs deep at Sebastian River High School. This week, alumni and coaches showed their school spirit through a new fundraising effort. Seventeen local businesses came together to raise more than $10,000 for new play clocks for the varsity football program.Coach Phinehas Weatherly said equipment issues have made it difficult to run an effective offense for years.WATCH BELOW: Businesses rally to buy high school new football equipment"For the last four years, it's been a battle of trying to get a working play clock, which is essential when you're trying to run an offense and keep it moving and not get delay games," Weatherly said.Weatherly said each repair cost thousands of dollars — a price a high school football program would struggle to keep up with. He turned to Facebook for help."I made a Facebook post saying, hey, I don't know who needs to hear this, but this is ridiculous. Not to compare us to other schools, but they get a lot of stuff and we can't even," Weatherly said.Shark alum Bryan Rhoades saw the post and took action, sharing his own video online asking the community to step up."I need five business owners or people, whoever, to match my $1,000. We can get this done," Rhoades said.Rhoades owns Airbnbs in the area along with River Ride Cart Rentals LLC. He offered to donate $1,000 and encouraged other businesses to do the same. The response was swift."Within like an hour I had $2,000 and within I think three more days we had $10,350," Rhoades said.The old play clocks were stationary and had suffered significant wear and tear over the years, requiring repeated electrical repairs and parts replacements. The new clocks are a much-needed and quality upgrade."They're lit up, they're bright and they're bigger than I thought, they're great. They roll around so they can keep them out of the weather. It's going to be great for the team," Rhoades said.For Weatherly, the community response meant more than just new equipment."For the longest time, it seemed like we were just getting pushed to the side. And to see that there's people out there that still care and want to support and want to help, you know, it was great. It was amazing," Weatherly said.Rhoades said the outpouring support reflected the character of the Sebastian community."They just want to get out there and help. That's what it comes down to really. You know what I mean, the kids," Rhoades said.Reminding everyone, a small act of kindness, or in this case Facebook post, can generate solutions to fix an old, costly problem."Everybody is out there still trying to help each other, still willing to give and be part of the community and make things better for the kids," Weatherly said.The new play clocks are expected to debut at Sebastian River's next home football game on Oct.

hero.headline: Former Fort Pierce city manager on trial for bid tampering in Lincoln Park project
hero.body:
Jury selection began Monday for former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms, who is accused of bid tampering and official misconduct tied to the Lincoln Park downtown corridor project.

Opening statements are expected Tuesday, with the trial expected to last through the end of the week, according to the State Attorney's Office. Mimms faces allegations that he rigged the bid process for the Lincoln Park downtown corridor. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement says Mimms gave a local nonprofit non-public information and controlled the language of the bid.

Two former city employees, including Mimms' niece, formed the nonprofit at the center of the investigation. The organization allegedly received confidential information that gave it an unfair advantage in the bidding process. Investigators say Mimms manipulated the bid requirements to favor the nonprofit connected to his family member.

Mimms has pleaded not guilty to the charges. The trial will determine whether the former city manager abused his position to steer city contracts to the organization with ties to his niece and another former municipal employee.

hero.headline: Pratt Whitney and Bridge Roads intersection backs up Martin County commuters
hero.body:
Drivers face significant delays at the intersection of Pratt Whitney and Bridge Roads in Martin County during morning and afternoon commute hours. The rural four-way stop backs up with commuters, particularly when accidents occur.

Many of those drivers travel from places like Lake Okeechobee and Pahokee. Workers who live far from their jobs in search of affordable housing make the long commute.

The intersection has received upgraded signs, rumble strips, and advanced warning signs. Installing a full traffic light requires meeting state thresholds for high traffic volumes or crash data. The county has studied widening the road in phases.

Breeze Airways launched four new nonstop routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport to East Coast destinations this week, with introductory fares starting at $74 one-way.

The airline began service to Trenton, New Jersey on Wednesday, operating flights on Wednesdays and Saturdays with one-way fares from $74. Service to Baltimore, Maryland and Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania launches Oct. 1, with flights on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Sundays. Baltimore fares start at $89 one-way, while Pittsburgh flights begin at $74 one-way. Atlantic City, New Jersey service starts Oct. 2 with flights on Mondays and Fridays, priced from $104 one-way.

The expansion gives Treasure Coast residents more convenient travel options to major metropolitan areas in the Northeast without having to connect through larger hub airports.

The airline earned spots on TIME Magazine's TIME100 Most Influential Companies list and Forbes' America's Best Brands for Value for 2026. Earlier this month, Breeze announced it will begin offering seasonal nonstop service from West Palm Beach to Greenville-Spartanburg, South Carolina starting in December.

Travelers can book flights at flybreeze.com or through the Breeze Airways mobile app.

hero.headline: Jury selection resumes in corruption trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms
hero.body:
Jury selection is set to resume Tuesday morning in the trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms, who is accused of manipulating a city bidding process to benefit a nonprofit connected to his niece. Prospective jurors were told to return to the St. Lucie County Courthouse by 8:30 a.m., with jury selection set to resume at 9 a.m. Judge Michael Linn said he hopes to seat a jury Tuesday and begin opening statements at 1:30 p.m.

Mimms, 53, has pleaded not guilty to charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. Prosecutors allege Mimms knowingly influenced the competitive bidding process in 2024 involving two city-owned lots at 1134 and 1138 Avenue D in Fort Pierce's Lincoln Park neighborhood.

Investigators say Mimms worked to ensure the lots would be leased by Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit connected to his niece, while concealing his alleged conflict of interest. The group planned to turn the vacant lots into a community space with a library, classrooms and space for small businesses. Authorities say the organization received information that other bidders did not have, helping it secure a low-cost, long-term lease from the city. The project was expected to receive funding through a $500,000 grant, but the lots remain vacant.

During jury selection Monday, prosecutor Jonathan Bridges asked prospective jurors whether they could listen to witnesses, review the evidence and decide whether bid tampering occurred. Potential jurors were also asked about their knowledge of Fort Pierce city government and whether they could presume Mimms innocent unless prosecutors prove the allegations beyond a reasonable doubt.

The trial is expected to last up to two weeks. If convicted on both charges, Mimms could face a combined maximum of 20 years in prison and $15,000 in fines.

hero.headline: Driver crashes into patrol vehicle in Indian River County, nearly hits deputy
hero.body:
A driver in Indian River County narrowly missed hitting a deputy before crashing into a patrol vehicle and driving into a ditch, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.

Two deputies were blocking a lane while a vehicle was being loaded onto a tow truck when the driver sped past, nearly striking one of the deputies, the sheriff's office said. The driver's truck then crashed into the back of a patrol vehicle before continuing into a ditch.

The driver was taken to a trauma center with non-life-threatening injuries. No deputies were injured, and no criminal charges have been filed.

Authorities reminded drivers to slow down and move over when they see flashing lights. Florida's Move Over law requires drivers to change lanes when approaching emergency vehicles, tow trucks, utility vehicles, and other service vehicles stopped on the roadside with flashing lights. When changing lanes is not possible, drivers must slow to a speed 20 miles per hour below the posted limit.

hero.headline: Opening statements begin in trial of former Fort Pierce city manager
hero.body:
Opening statements began Tuesday in the trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms, who faces charges of bid tampering and official misconduct involving city-owned properties and a nonprofit linked to his niece.

Prosecutors told jurors they would present emails, witness testimony, and city documents to support their case. They alleged Mimms used his position to influence the bidding process for the development of city-owned properties.

"Mimms carefully, skillfully steered the bid for the development of this property so that it would end up in the hands of two city employees. And one of those employees was Mr. Mimms' niece," prosecutor Bridges said.

Mimms is accused of helping Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit founded by his niece, secure a lease to develop two city-owned properties.

Defense attorney Donald Murrell described Mimms' relationship with his niece as distant.

"The state puts a lot of emphasis on the fact that she is my client's niece, and she is, but she can fairly be called a distant niece if that's at all possible," Murrell said.

The defense argued that Mimms did not conspire to commit the crime.

"If you follow the law, you follow the facts, and we're comfortable at the end of this case you will find that Mr. Mimms is not guilty," Murrell said.

The state also called its first witness. Several city officials, including the mayor, are expected to testify.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie approves 11th straight property tax rate cut despite rapid growth
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate as part of a $971.6 million budget. The tax cut continues despite more than 60,000 new residents moving to the city since 2020.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning in October as part of the city's $971.6 million budget. The council made the decision during the formal budget adoption on Monday.

The tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services.

Since 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value. The trend of tax relief has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.

"Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," Mayor Shannon Martin said. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."

The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners. The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.

The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

hero.headline: Two new Florida laws close loopholes in child exploitation, animal cruelty statutes
hero.body:
Two new Florida laws taking effect October 1 will impose tougher penalties on adults who exploit children by closing loopholes in existing statutes, though child advocates say emerging threats from artificial intelligence and deepfakes remain unaddressed.

House Bill 1525 makes it a third-degree felony for indecent exposure or non-contact sexual acts performed in front of a minor under 16, even if the child was unaware of or did not see the act. Child advocates say the law addresses a loophole that has been used in the defense of lewd or lascivious behavior.

Sarah Marie Henry, executive director of Catch the Wave of Hope and an expert in child exploitation, said the change is significant. "Now, this is closing that loophole which is really great because whether a child was fully aware or sleeping or not it is obviously really unsafe behavior to do around a child," Henry said.

House Bill 559 makes it a third-degree felony for someone 18 or older to force or entice a minor to commit animal cruelty. The law also penalizes an adult who performs animal cruelty in front of a minor. "We love to see that because we know and we agree that children of course especially in cases like this should not be involved or coerced to do these types of things," Henry said.

While Henry commends Florida lawmakers for the steps taken to protect children, she said emerging threats still need to be addressed. "I think we're going to see a lot more of it to come especially when we're talking about the AI side and the deep fakes and the progression of this child sexual abuse material that is out there," Henry said.

Both laws are among more than a dozen set to take effect in Florida on October 1.

hero.headline: Jury selection underway in Fort Pierce corruption trial of former city manager Nick Mimms
hero.body:
Jury selection is underway in the trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Nick Mimms, more than two years after his arrest on bid tampering and official misconduct charges tied to a city bidding process involving two vacant, city-owned lots in the Lincoln Park area.

Prospective jurors are being asked in court what they know about the case, if they've reached any conclusions about Mimms' guilt or innocence, and if they can put aside any information they may have heard or read about the case and base their verdict solely on the evidence presented in the courtroom. Prospective jurors were told Monday the trial may take one to two weeks.

Mimms, 53, was arrested in August 2024. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement accused Mimms of using his position to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals secure a lease for the lots. Investigators said the nonprofit was formed by two city employees, including Mimms' niece.

Investigators also accused Mimms, who served as project manager for the request for proposals, of influencing the language and evaluation criteria used in the bidding process and sharing nonpublic information with the nonprofit before the bid became public. The property, located at 1134 and 1138 Avenue D, was intended to become a community center called The Root, with plans that included a library, classroom space and pop-up markets. Mimms had served as Fort Pierce city manager since 2015 after previously working as deputy city manager and project engineer for the city. Outside the courtroom Monday, Mimms had no comment.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce ex-city manager trial opens with bid rigging allegations
hero.body:
Testimony began Tuesday in the trial of Nick Mimms, the former Fort Pierce city manager accused of rigging a bid process for city-owned land in Lincoln Park to favor a nonprofit tied to his niece.

Prosecutor Bridges told the court that Mimms ensured the city-owned land would ultimately be leased by Lincoln Park Young Professionals and no one else. The nonprofit, known as LPYP, received a $500,000 grant from the Alleghany Franciscan Ministries toward development of the site.

Defense attorney Donald Murrell countered that Mimms showed no favoritism and that the grant did not involve the city. Murrell said the project failed but not through deliberate action by any one person.

The state called its first witness, Ben Masondo, a local real estate broker from the Doyen Company who also submitted a bid on the two vacant lots. Masondo testified he felt the city's decision to move forward with LPYP was unfair.

"You have one that has a city employee involved. I felt that the judging was misguided. At one point, I think I had said clearly one of these people was the Russian judge, just decided not to score me fairly, and I looked at what was around, and yes, I was upset. They snaked me," Masondo said.

The trial is expected to last at least a week.

If found guilty, Mimms could face a second-degree felony for bid tampering that carries a maximum of 15 years in prison and up to a $10,000 fine. Official misconduct is a third-degree felony that carries a maximum of five years in prison and up to a $5,000 fine.

hero.headline: Martin County to decide Oct. 13 if Waterside qualifies under agricultural enclave law
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners will hold a public hearing October 13 to decide whether 396 acres near Kanner Highway qualify as an agricultural enclave under a new state law, one year after they rejected a residential proposal for the same land. Certification would allow the developer to later submit housing plans for up to 1,200 homes without another commission vote.

Kanner/96th Street Investments LLC has asked commissioners to certify the property, known as Waterside, under a state law that took effect July 1. Florida business records list The Kolter Group as the LLC's manager. The property lies south of SW 96th Street, between Kanner Highway and the St. Lucie River. Commissioners voted 5-0 in November 2025 not to advance a request to change the land's designation from agricultural to low-density residential.

Senior Planner Jenna Knobbe said the application requests a density of about 3.1 homes per acre, or roughly 1,200 single-family homes. That is a proposed figure, not an approved home count. "We have no comment at this time," Harvey said in an email.

The law is meant for certain agricultural properties that are already surrounded by development or land planned for it. To qualify, an applicant must meet specific requirements involving the property's agricultural history, surrounding land, size and access to services such as roads, water and sewer. Commissioners can deny certification if the land does not qualify, but they must base their decision on the law's criteria, not simply whether they want homes built there. A denial requires written findings, which the applicant can challenge in court. If the county takes no action within 90 days of receiving an application, state law says the land must be certified.

"It does take away some of the local control for local governments for deciding where development may or may not take place," Knobbe said in an interview. She said certification is the only part of this process that would go before commissioners. If certified, the property owner could submit development plans for administrative review without another commission hearing or vote on those plans.

The property is outside the county's urban service district, where the county generally directs more intensive development and plans for supporting services. "The county had not necessarily planned for that level of development on these properties," Knobbe said. Roads, drainage, water and sewer would still need review. Knobbe said the county would need to negotiate with the developer over who pays for any needed infrastructure improvements.

Greg Braun, executive director of The Guardians of Martin County, said his organization wants development to follow the county's existing growth plan. "Tallahassee legislators seem to think that they know better about what's going on locally than our local elected officials, and we think that that's wrong," Braun said.

Gil Smart, advocacy director for Friends of the Everglades, said his organization opposed the law because of concerns about development and public involvement. "People value the open space, the green space, as they see them being taken away and bulldozed flat so we can build more housing," Smart said. "People are going to have something to say about that, and they need to have a say in that."

Commissioners unanimously approved fees for reviewing applications under the new law: $8,150 to review whether property qualifies and $16,600 to review development plans submitted later. Knobbe said the law puts staff on a tight schedule. The county has 30 days to review a certification application and issue a report. A public hearing must follow within another 30 days. "We've kind of had to drop everything that we're working on and prioritize that application," Knobbe told commissioners Tuesday. A separate deadline would apply if the land is certified and the applicant submits development plans: County staff would have no more than 180 days to review them. "These are very expedited timeframes for what we typically will do for a major development plan type of review, because there's a lot of moving parts," Knobbe said.

cards.headline: Driver killed in fiery I-95 North crash in Martin County; lanes closed 7 hours
cards.teaser: A Honda Civic driver died Monday morning after colliding with the rear of a box truck on I-95 North at mile marker 91 in Martin County. The crash closed all northbound lanes for over seven hours.
cards.body:
A driver died Monday morning after a sedan collided with a box truck on Interstate 95 North in Martin County, shutting down all northbound lanes for over seven hours.

The crash occurred at around 3:40 a.m. at mile marker 91, involving a Honda Civic and a Hino box truck. According to the Florida Highway Patrol, both vehicles were traveling northbound when the Honda Civic collided with the rear of the box truck in the outside lane.

The sedan lodged underneath the back of the box truck and engulfed in flames. Despite lifesaving efforts, the Honda driver was pronounced deceased on scene. The driver of the box truck was not injured in the crash.

FHP has not identified the deceased driver. All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed until just before 11 a.m.

According to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP), both vehicles were traveling northbound when the Honda Civic collided with the rear of the box truck in the outside lane. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie cuts property tax rate for 11th straight year
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1. The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade. The new rate takes effect Thursday.

Since 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, giving the city the third lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value. The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.

Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services. The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.

"Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," said Mayor Shannon M. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible." The reduction marks another year of tax relief for Port St. Lucie residents as the city balances growth demands with fiscal responsibility.

Commissioners can deny certification if the land does not qualify based on specific requirements involving agricultural history, surrounding land, size and access to services such as roads, water and sewer. But they must base their decision on the law's criteria, not simply whether they want homes built there. A denial requires written findings, which the applicant can challenge in court. If the county takes no action within 90 days of receiving an application, state law says the land must be certified.

Certification would not approve a subdivision. But it would let the applicant later submit qualifying housing plans based on what is allowed on neighboring land. The law says those plans must be treated as an allowed use even if the county's existing growth plan or zoning would otherwise prohibit it. County staff would still review the plans, but the law does not require another commission hearing on them.

"It does take away some of the local control for local governments for deciding where development may or may not take place," Knobbe said. She said certification is the only part of this process that would go before commissioners. If certified, the property owner could submit development plans for administrative review without another commission hearing or vote on those plans.

The property is outside the county's urban service district, where the county generally directs more intensive development and plans for supporting services. Knobbe said the county had not necessarily planned for that level of development on these properties. Roads, drainage, water and sewer would still need review. The county would need to negotiate with the developer over who pays for any needed infrastructure improvements.

Martin County has long tried to keep new neighborhoods from spreading into rural areas. Greg Braun, executive director of The Guardians of Martin County, said his organization wants development to follow the county's existing growth plan. "Tallahassee legislators seem to think that they know better about what's going on locally than our local elected officials, and we think that that's wrong," Braun said.

Gil Smart, advocacy director for Friends of the Everglades, said his organization opposed the law because of concerns about development and public involvement. "People value the open space, the green space, as they see them being taken away and bulldozed flat so we can build more housing," Smart said. "People are going to have something to say about that, and they need to have a say in that."

Commissioners on Tuesday unanimously approved fees for reviewing applications under the new law: $8,150 to review whether property qualifies and $16,600 to review development plans submitted later. Knobbe said the law puts staff on a tight schedule. The county has 30 days to review a certification application and issue a report. A public hearing must follow within another 30 days. "We've kind of had to drop everything that we're working on and prioritize that application," Knobbe told commissioners.

A separate deadline would apply if the land is certified and the applicant submits development plans: County staff would have no more than 180 days to review them. "These are very expedited timeframes for what we typically will do for a major development plan type of review, because there's a lot of moving parts," Knobbe said.

"We have no comment at this time," Harvey said.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach Boulevard closed after construction crew strikes gas line
cards.teaser: Jensen Beach Boulevard is closed from NE Skyline Drive west to NE Highland Avenue after a construction crew struck a gas line Monday, prompting evacuations of nearby businesses.
cards.body:
Jensen Beach Boulevard is closed after a construction crew working in the area struck a gas line Monday, officials said. The closure extends along Jensen Beach Boulevard from NE Skyline Drive west to NE Highland Avenue as crews work to repair the damaged line and secure the area.

Officials said nearby businesses have been notified of the incident, and several businesses in the area have been evacuated as a precaution while emergency crews respond. No injuries have been reported.

Motorists are urged to avoid the area and seek alternate routes. Drivers should allow extra travel time and follow any posted detours until the roadway reopens.

Authorities anticipate the road closure will remain in place for several hours as repair work continues and safety assessments are completed.

hero.headline: New calculator estimates Amendment 3 would cut $7 million in St. Lucie County road funding
hero.body:
The Florida Policy Institute has launched an online tool estimating that Amendment 3 would cut $7 million in road funding for St. Lucie County if voters approve the property tax exemption measure in November. The Local Funding Cuts Calculator provides budget impact estimates for all 67 Florida counties and represents a new level of detail in analyzing the amendment's potential effects. Amendment 3 is a referendum that aims to raise the homestead exemption to lower property tax bills for homeowners.

"It goes beyond counties and cities; it touches special districts, which has not been noted or spoken to with previous tools. Floridians deserve to have more information," Esteban Santis, research director at FPI, said. The tool includes data on special districts in addition to counties and cities, offering a broader view of how the amendment could affect various government services across the state. According to Sadah Knight, the CEO of Florida Policy Institute, "Vital services in every part of our state will be impacted."

The calculator shows other examples of potential budget impacts throughout the region, including a $28 million effect on conservation and water management in Palm Beach County and $455,000 for children's services in Okeechobee County. These estimates reflect how the property tax exemption could reduce funding for specific services that local governments and special districts currently provide. The tool allows residents to see projected impacts specific to their counties and the various services those areas provide.

Supporters of Amendment 3 argue the measure addresses affordability concerns facing Florida residents. "Everywhere you look, people are feeling the pinch of affordability, and Amendment 3 has the opportunity to return more money back to the taxpayers," Margy Grant of the Florida Realtors Association said. The amendment would increase the homestead exemption, resulting in lower property tax bills for homeowners across the state. However, the Florida Policy Institute's calculator highlights the tradeoff, showing how reduced property tax revenue would translate into cuts for local government services ranging from road maintenance to environmental conservation and social services. Voters will decide on the measure in November.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie cuts property tax rate for 11th straight year despite 60,000 new residents
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1. The decision came during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday.

The tax cuts continue despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services.

Since 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value. The reduction has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.

"Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," Mayor Shannon M. said. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."

The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.

The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low. The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man charged with trafficking, weapons counts after Fields Avenue raid
cards.teaser: Bruce Alexander Francis, 30, faces a $530,000 bond on multiple charges including methamphetamine trafficking and weapons possession after a SWAT search warrant execution at his home last week.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie SWAT team served a search warrant at a Fields Avenue home last week and arrested Bruce Alexander Francis, 30, on charges including methamphetamine trafficking, cocaine possession with intent to sell, weapons possession, and identity theft following an undercover cocaine buy. His bond was set at $530,000 on Tuesday.

SWAT officers executed the warrant about 5:30 a.m. Sept. 22 at 406 SW Fields Ave., where Francis and five other people exited the home. Francis told detectives that any drugs in the home belonged to him but declined to provide further information. He denied having a phone, though investigators said they found the cellphone used in a prior cocaine transaction.

Police used a confidential informant earlier in September to buy about 3.5 grams of cocaine from Francis at the home. The substance later tested presumptively positive for cocaine and weighed about 4 grams. Francis was also charged with selling cocaine and using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony in that case.

A woman told police she shared the master bedroom with Francis and a baby. She said Francis stayed home with the children during the day and that she did not know what he did for work. Detectives said they found suspected cocaine in the master bedroom and bathroom, including bags in and around a toilet. SWAT officers reported seeing Francis run from the bedroom to the bathroom and throw something before closing the door.

Police reported finding a Fanta bottle containing a green liquid in the refrigerator that tested presumptively positive for methamphetamine. The liquid weighed about 180.5 grams.

The search also turned up $2,560 in cash, a .22-caliber revolver, .22-caliber and 9mm ammunition, scales, plastic baggies, suspected marijuana and THC products. In the master bedroom closet and elsewhere in the home, police said they found driver's licenses, Social Security cards, debit cards and credit cards belonging to several other people. The report identifies documents belonging to people in Texas and Florida.

Francis was charged with trafficking in methamphetamine, possession of cocaine with intent to sell, marijuana possession, possession of drug equipment, three counts of possessing another person's identification without consent, evidence tampering and two counts of possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon. Police said Francis had a 2014 felony conviction.

In the master bedroom closet and elsewhere in the home, police said they found driver's licenses, Social Security cards, debit cards and credit cards belonging to several other people. The report identifies documents belonging to people in Texas and Florida.

Police said Francis had a 2014 felony conviction.

cards.headline: Indiantown residents challenge Martin County Sheriff over no charges in bus stop gun incident
cards.teaser: Residents packed a community meeting Monday night to demand answers after a father who pulled a gun on two students at an Indiantown bus stop was not charged with a crime.
cards.body:
Residents packed a community meeting Monday night to demand answers from the Martin County Sheriff's Office after a father who pulled a gun on two students at an Indiantown bus stop was not charged with a crime.

The tense meeting, led by the Martin County NAACP and Sheriff John Budensiek, centered on the sheriff's determination that the father acted in self-defense. Many residents argued that the man should have been arrested for the separate crime of possessing a firearm at a school bus stop.

Budensiek laid out his office's account of the incident, which occurred just over a week ago. He said it began with a student being bullied and struck by another student on a school bus. The victim's father went to the bus stop to report the bullying to the driver. The situation escalated when the alleged bully and a friend pushed past the bus driver and tried to confront the father.

"He puts his hand up and backs up, backs up, says 'stay away, stay away,' and they don't," Budensiek said. "In fact, they're yelling that they're going to whoop his hind end... He pulls out a gun and all of a sudden they're backing up, because they don't want to get shot."

The sheriff defended the lack of charges against the father, citing the state's self-defense laws. "In the state of Florida, you're allowed to defend yourself against someone coming after you," he said.

Residents at the meeting argued that the father was committing a misdemeanor by possessing a gun at a bus stop, which they believe should negate his Stand Your Ground defense. "Stand Your Ground cannot come into play because at the time you were committing a crime by being at that bus stop with a gun," one resident yelled.

Budensiek countered that the law does not provide a clear legal definition of what constitutes a bus stop, making that specific charge unenforceable in this case. The father declined to press battery charges against the two students.

Jimmy Smith, President of the Martin County NAACP, said the meeting was intended to inform the community about the laws that guided the sheriff's decision. He urged residents who are unhappy with the outcome to channel their anger toward changing those laws.

"These kids need to be loved and also protected on all ends," Smith said after the meeting. "Thank God nobody went home in a casket."

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie cuts property tax rate for 11th straight year
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1. The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.

Since 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value.

Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services.

Mayor Shannon M. said the city aims to provide the services residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars. By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, the city has been able to continue meeting the needs of the growing community while remaining fiscally responsible, the mayor said.

The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low. The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.

The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

hero.headline: Martin County residents demand charges in Indiantown bus stop gun incident at heated NAACP meeting
hero.body:
Martin County residents packed a community meeting Monday night to demand charges against a father who pulled a gun on two students at an Indiantown bus stop, arguing that possessing a firearm at that location should have barred his self-defense claim. Sheriff John Budensiek defended the no-charge decision but acknowledged the law does not clearly define what constitutes a bus stop.

The tense meeting, led by the Martin County NAACP and the sheriff, centered on the incident that occurred just over a week ago. Budensiek said the confrontation began when a student was bullied and struck by another student on a school bus. The victim's father went to the bus stop to report the bullying to the driver.

The situation escalated when the alleged bully and a friend pushed past the bus driver and tried to confront the father, Budensiek said. The father backed up and told them to stay away, but the students continued approaching and yelled that they were going to whoop his hind end, the sheriff said. The father then pulled out a gun and the students backed away.

Budensiek cited state self-defense laws to justify the decision not to charge the father. "In the state of Florida, you're allowed to defend yourself against someone coming after you," he said.

Residents argued the father was committing a misdemeanor by possessing a gun at a bus stop, which they believe should negate his Stand Your Ground defense. "Stand Your Ground cannot come into play because at the time you were committing a crime by being at that bus stop with a gun," one resident yelled.

Budensiek countered that the law does not provide a clear legal definition of what constitutes a bus stop, making that specific charge unenforceable in this case. The father declined to press battery charges against the two students.

Jimmy Smith, President of the Martin County NAACP, said the meeting was intended to inform the community about the laws that guided the sheriff's decision. He urged residents who are unhappy with the outcome to channel their anger toward changing those laws.

"These kids need to be loved and also protected on all ends," Smith said after the meeting. "Thank God nobody went home in a casket."

Smith said that while there was disagreement, everyone shared one sentiment: "We can agree that this should have never happened."

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie schedules removal of 18 Flock cameras by Sept. 30
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie will remove 18 Flock cameras installed in county and state rights-of-way by Sept. 30, city officials said Monday as the automated license plate reader program remains paused amid privacy concerns and a pending federal lawsuit.

City officials confirmed the removal date during a City Council meeting where residents urged a permanent ban on the cameras. The 18 cameras scheduled for removal include nine installed in county rights-of-way and nine in state rights-of-way. A city staff member told the council the vendor will remove the cameras by the Sept. 30 deadline. Port St. Lucie police announced Sept. 1 that the department would pause the program and remove seven cameras.

Residents Casey Honeycutt and Jorge Borgess called for a citywide ban on Flock cameras and similar automated vehicle-tracking systems. Borgess asked the city to stop issuing permits for automated license plate readers in city-owned or city-controlled rights-of-way and to pursue removal of existing cameras. Steven Grier told the council he has sued the city, Mayor Shannon Martin and Flock in federal court. James Reynolds told council members the city had previously achieved its public safety goals without Flock cameras.

Councilman John Bonna said the city needs to address misuse penalties and retention periods before resuming the program. "We need to make sure there's punishments for misuse; we need to make sure that retention periods are addressed; our audit is complete," Bonna said. "I know there have been local incidents of misuse, and so this isn't something abstract." Bonna said he was calling for a pause, not immediate removal of all cameras. "What I'm calling for is to pause the program, and when I say pause, I mean pause, and let's get this policy right, so it protects both our liberties and safety," Bonna said.

The city paused the program after the Florida Department of Transportation revoked approvals for the technology in state highway rights-of-way. The pause limits use of remaining systems to cases involving an immediate threat to life, including missing or endangered people, with authorization from Police Chief Leo Niemczyk. Earlier this month, St. Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to stop new permits for Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers in county-controlled rights-of-way, review existing permits and issue removal notices where appropriate. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said his office would comply with the state directive while tightening internal rules for deputies' use of the technology.

hero.headline: Indiantown meeting erupts over no charges in bus stop gun incident
hero.body:
A packed community meeting in Indiantown turned contentious Monday night as residents confronted Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek over his decision not to charge a father who pulled a gun on two students at a bus stop, with many arguing the man should have been arrested for the separate crime of possessing a firearm at a school bus stop.

The meeting, led by the Martin County NAACP and the sheriff, centered on an incident just over a week ago in which a father went to a bus stop to report that his child had been bullied and struck by another student on the school bus. Budensiek said the situation escalated when the alleged bully and a friend pushed past the bus driver and tried to confront the father, who backed up and told them to stay away. When they continued advancing and yelled threats, the father pulled out a gun and the students backed away.

Budensiek defended the lack of charges by citing state self-defense laws, saying the father was allowed to defend himself. But residents at the meeting argued that the father was committing a misdemeanor by possessing a gun at a bus stop, which they believe should negate his Stand Your Ground defense. "Stand Your Ground cannot come into play because at the time you were committing a crime by being at that bus stop with a gun," one resident yelled. The sheriff countered that the law does not provide a clear legal definition of what constitutes a bus stop, making that specific charge unenforceable in this case.

Jimmy Smith, President of the Martin County NAACP, said the meeting was intended to inform the community about the laws that guided the sheriff's decision. He urged residents who are unhappy with the outcome to channel their anger toward changing those laws. "These kids need to be loved and also protected on all ends," Smith said after the meeting. "Thank God nobody went home in a casket." He said that while there was disagreement, everyone shared one sentiment: "We can agree that this should have never happened." The father declined to press battery charges against the two students.

hero.headline: Florida executes 77-year-old Curtis Beasley, state's 16th this year
hero.body:
Florida executed Curtis Wilkie Beasley on Tuesday evening, marking the state's 16th execution this year in what has become the nation's busiest death chamber. Beasley, 77, received a lethal injection at the state prison starting at 6 p.m. for the 1995 murder of Carolyn Monfort. The execution came as a separate competency review has paused the next scheduled execution of William Lee Thompson, 74, who is set for Oct. 13.

Beasley was convicted of first-degree murder, robbery and grand theft auto after beating Monfort to death with a hammer at her Dundee home south of Orlando in August 1995. He had been staying at the home while pressure washing and painting apartments owned by her son-in-law. Monfort's daughter found her body in a blood-splattered laundry room after being unable to reach her for two days. Monfort suffered multiple blunt-force trauma injuries to the head, and a bloody hammer head was found wrapped in a towel nearby.

Authorities arrested Beasley in Alabama, where he was working under a fake name for an electrical company after traveling from Miami. He was convicted of murder and sentenced to death in 1998. The Florida Supreme Court last week rejected appeals that executing a man his age suffering from cognitive decline would amount to cruel and unusual punishment. A final appeal remained pending before the U.S. Supreme Court.

Beasley became the seventh Florida prisoner over the age of 70 executed this year and the nation's 29th execution this year. The state executed 19 people last year, a record since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.

Gov. Ron DeSantis temporarily paused Thompson's Oct. 13 execution after a doctor this month determined Thompson might be suffering from dementia. DeSantis ordered a panel of three psychiatrists to examine Thompson on Thursday to determine if he is competent to be executed. Thompson was convicted of raping and fatally beating a woman at a Florida motel in 1976. DeSantis issued similar stays in 2023 and 2025, but both executions proceeded following evaluations.

William Reaves, 77, has an execution scheduled for October. He was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy outside a convenience store in 1986. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart.

hero.headline: Indiantown residents erupt at NAACP meeting over gun at bus stop, no charges
hero.body:
Indiantown residents packed a community meeting Monday night to challenge the Martin County Sheriff's Office decision not to charge a father who pulled a gun on two students at a bus stop, arguing that the man should have been arrested for possessing a firearm at the location regardless of his self-defense claim.

The meeting, led by the Martin County NAACP and Sheriff John Budensiek, grew tense as residents disputed whether Florida's Stand Your Ground law should apply when the father was allegedly committing a misdemeanor by having a gun at a school bus stop. The incident occurred just over a week ago.

Budensiek said the confrontation began when a student who had been bullied and struck on a bus told his father, who went to the bus stop to report the incident to the driver. The alleged bully and a friend pushed past the driver and tried to confront the father, the sheriff said. The father backed up and said "stay away, stay away," but the two students continued advancing and yelled they were going to whoop him, Budensiek explained. The father then pulled out a gun and the students backed away.

"In the state of Florida, you're allowed to defend yourself against someone coming after you," Budensiek said, defending the decision not to charge the father.

Residents erupted in anger, with one shouting that Stand Your Ground cannot apply because the father was committing a crime by being at the bus stop with a gun. Budensiek countered that the law does not provide a clear legal definition of what constitutes a bus stop, making that specific charge unenforceable in this case. The father declined to press battery charges against the two students.

Jimmy Smith, President of the Martin County NAACP, said the meeting was intended to inform the community about the laws that guided the sheriff's decision. He urged residents who are unhappy with the outcome to work toward changing those laws.

"These kids need to be loved and also protected on all ends," Smith said after the meeting. "Thank God nobody went home in a casket."

Smith said that while there was disagreement, everyone shared one sentiment: "We can agree that this should have never happened."

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man called 911 to confess stabbing of 79-year-old father
cards.teaser: Cartavion Jermaine Merritt told dispatchers he used two knives to stab his father in the chest with intent to kill. The victim, initially airlifted with life-threatening injuries, was later reported in stable condition.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man who was arrested Sunday night after stabbing his 79-year-old father called 911 himself to report the attack and confess, telling dispatchers he intended to kill the victim, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. The victim, initially airlifted with life-threatening injuries, was later reported in stable condition. Cartavion Jermaine Merritt now faces charges of attempted homicide-murder without premeditation and aggravated battery on a person 65 years of age or older.

Cartavion Jermaine Merritt, 44, called 911 late Sunday to report the stabbing at a home in the 11200 block of NW Blockbird Drive, according to police. Merritt told dispatchers he used two knives to stab the man in the chest and stated his intention was to kill him. He told dispatchers that only he and the victim were inside the home and that he had placed the two knives used in the attack in the kitchen sink.

Officers arrived and Merritt exited the home voluntarily and was arrested without incident. Once Merritt was secured, officers entered the residence and found the elderly victim suffering from three stab wounds to the upper chest. Officers and paramedics immediately began providing life-saving medical care before the victim was airlifted to the hospital.

Investigators found the two knives in the sink and determined the stabbing happened in the bedroom where blood was found on the sheets. During questioning at the police department, Merritt admitted that his intent during the incident was to kill the victim, according to police.

hero.headline: Indiantown residents confront Martin County sheriff over no charges in bus stop gun incident
hero.body:
Residents packed a community meeting in Indiantown Tuesday night and confronted the Martin County Sheriff's Office over the decision not to charge a parent who pulled a gun on two students at a bus stop, with many arguing the man should have been arrested for possessing a firearm at the location.

The tense meeting, led by the Martin County NAACP and Sheriff John Budensiek, centered on whether the father's self-defense claim should have been negated by the separate crime of gun possession at a school bus stop. Residents yelled that Stand Your Ground laws cannot apply when someone is committing a misdemeanor at the time. The sheriff defended his decision not to file charges, explaining that the incident began when a student was bullied and struck by another student on a school bus. The victim's father went to the bus stop to report the bullying to the driver, but the situation escalated when the alleged bully and a friend pushed past the bus driver to confront the father. "He puts his hand up and backs up, backs up, says 'stay away, stay away,' and they don't," Budensiek explained. "In fact, they're yelling that they're going to whoop his hind end... He pulls out a gun and all of a sudden they're backing up, because they don't want to get shot."

Budensiek cited Florida's self-defense laws as justification for the decision, saying the state allows people to defend themselves against someone coming after them. However, he acknowledged the gun possession issue, stating that the law does not provide a clear legal definition of what constitutes a bus stop, making that specific charge unenforceable in this case. The father also declined to press battery charges against the two students who allegedly confronted him.

Jimmy Smith, President of the Martin County NAACP, said the meeting was intended to inform the community about the laws that guided the sheriff's decision. He urged residents who are unhappy with the outcome to channel their anger toward changing those laws. "These kids need to be loved and also protected on all ends," Smith said after the meeting. "Thank God nobody went home in a casket." Smith acknowledged the disagreement in the room but said everyone shared one sentiment about the incident. "We can agree that this should have never happened," he said.

Indiantown residents packed a community meeting Tuesday night to demand answers from the Martin County Sheriff's Office after a parent who pulled a gun on two students at a bus stop was not charged with a crime.

The tense meeting, led by the Martin County NAACP and Sheriff John Budensiek, centered on the sheriff's determination that the father acted in self-defense. Many residents argued the man should have been arrested for the separate crime of possessing a firearm at a school bus stop.

Budensiek laid out his office's account of the incident, which occurred just over a week ago. He said it began with a student being bullied and struck by another student on a school bus. The victim's father went to the bus stop to report the bullying to the driver. The situation escalated when the alleged bully and a friend pushed past the bus driver and tried to confront the father.

"He puts his hand up and backs up, backs up, says 'stay away, stay away,' and they don't," Budensiek explained. "In fact, they're yelling that they're going to whoop his hind end... He pulls out a gun and all of a sudden they're backing up, because they don't want to get shot."

The sheriff defended the lack of charges, citing the state's self-defense laws. "In the state of Florida, you're allowed to defend yourself against someone coming after you," he said.

Residents were furious, arguing that the father was committing a misdemeanor by possessing a gun at a bus stop, which they believe should negate his Stand Your Ground defense. "Stand Your Ground cannot come into play because at the time you were committing a crime by being at that bus stop with a gun," one resident yelled.

Budensiek countered that the law does not provide a clear legal definition of what constitutes a bus stop, making that specific charge unenforceable in this case. The father also declined to press battery charges against the two students.

Jimmy Smith, President of the Martin County NAACP, said the meeting was intended to inform the community about the laws that guided the sheriff's decision. He urged residents who are unhappy with the outcome to channel their anger toward changing those laws.

"These kids need to be loved and also protected on all ends," Smith said after the meeting. "Thank God nobody went home in a casket."

cards.teaser: All northbound lanes of Interstate 95 in Martin County reopened Monday afternoon after a seven-hour closure following a fatal early-morning crash involving a car and a box truck.
cards.body:
All northbound lanes of Interstate 95 in Martin County reopened Monday afternoon after a seven-hour closure following a fatal early-morning crash involving a car and a box truck that killed the car's driver.

The crash happened around 4 a.m. north of Jupiter near Bridge Road, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. Investigators said the front of a car hit the back of a box truck while both vehicles were traveling northbound, causing the car to catch fire.

The driver of the car was pronounced dead at the scene. The driver of the box truck was not injured.

hero.headline: Jury selection opens in bid-tampering trial of former Fort Pierce city manager
hero.body:
Jury selection began Monday in the trial of former Fort Pierce city manager Nicholas Mimms, who is accused of bid tampering and official misconduct related to city-owned properties. Judge Michael Lynn oversaw the process at the St. Lucie County Courthouse, where 60 potential jurors were considered. Several individuals were not selected because they either knew Mimms, had worked with him, or cited medical or financial hardships.

Mimms is facing allegations of using his position to manipulate a bidding process involving two vacant city-owned lots in Fort Pierce's Lincoln Park area. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms ensured that a nonprofit organization called Lincoln Park Young Professionals received a lease to develop the two properties. FDLE investigators said the nonprofit was formed by Mimms' niece.

The trial is expected to last two weeks.

hero.headline: Fatal I-95 crash in Martin County closes northbound lanes for over seven hours
hero.teaser: A Honda Civic slammed into the rear of a box truck and caught fire early Monday morning on Interstate 95 North at mile marker 91 in Martin County, killing the sedan driver and shutting down all northbound lanes until just before 11 a.m.
hero.body:
A Honda Civic slammed into the rear of a box truck and caught fire early Monday morning on Interstate 95 North at mile marker 91 in Martin County, killing the sedan driver and shutting down all northbound lanes until just before 11 a.m.

The crash occurred around 3:40 a.m. Both vehicles were traveling northbound when the Honda Civic collided with the rear of the Hino box truck in the outside lane, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The sedan lodged underneath the back of the box truck and engulfed in flames. Despite lifesaving efforts, the Honda driver was pronounced deceased on scene.

The driver of the box truck was not injured. FHP has not identified the deceased driver. All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed for over seven hours.

According to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP), both vehicles were traveling northbound when the Honda Civic collided with the rear of the box truck in the outside lane. The sedan lodged underneath the back of the tractor-trailer and engulfed in flames. Despite lifesaving efforts, the Honda driver was pronounced deceased on scene. The driver of the box truck was not injured in the crash. FHP has not identified the deceased driver. All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed until just before 11 a.m.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Council votes Monday on $971.6M budget, lower tax rate
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council is scheduled to take a final vote Monday on a $971.6 million budget for fiscal year 2026-27 and a reduced property tax rate of 4.8750 mills, down from 4.9750. The final budget hearing is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. at Port St. Lucie City Hall, immediately following the 5 p.m. Community Redevelopment Agency meeting.

Council members are expected to take second and final readings on both the millage rate and budget ordinances. The new fiscal year begins Oct. 1.

A mill is equal to $1 in property taxes for every $1,000 of taxable property value. At 4.875 mills, that works out to about $4.88 in city property taxes for every $1,000 of taxable value. A homeowner's final bill also depends on the taxable value of the property and taxes charged by other local taxing authorities. For homeowners, a lower millage rate does not automatically mean a lower property tax bill.

Monday's vote comes after city leaders spent the summer tightening the budget amid concerns about possible future losses in property tax revenue. During a July budget workshop, City Manager Jesus Merejo told council members Port St. Lucie could lose more than $48 million in property tax revenue over two years if a proposed state constitutional amendment is approved by voters in November.

As part of its preparations, the city left 184 requested positions unfunded, worth about $28.3 million. That included 25 proposed police officer positions. The city also cut about $7.8 million in planned projects, including a study for a new interchange connecting Marshall Parkway to Interstate 95, an inclusive playground at McChesney Park and parking improvements at Riverland Paseo Park.

The proposed 4.8750 millage rate includes a reduction in both the city's operating millage and the voter-approved debt millage tied to Crosstown Parkway.

hero.headline: Vero Beach parking fines double Oct. 1 for fire lanes, hydrants, tow-away zones
hero.body:
Vero Beach parking fines will double on several violations beginning Oct. 1. The Vero Beach Police Department announced the increases Sunday.

Parking in a fire lane, blocking a fire hydrant, and parking in an emergency-vehicles-only tow-away zone will each rise from $30 to $60. Fines for improper parking that obstructs traffic and other parking violations will also increase from $30 to $60. Overtime parking and parking over a line will rise from $20 to $40.

The Vero Beach Police Department urged drivers to review the updated fine schedule before the new penalties take effect Wednesday.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested after stabbing 79-year-old father three times
hero.body:
A 44-year-old Port St. Lucie man stabbed his 79-year-old father three times in the chest and admitted to authorities that he wanted to kill him, according to police. Cartavion Merritt was arrested Sunday at a home on NW Blackbird Drive after calling 911 himself. Body camera footage captured officers responding to the scene.

"Our suspect was actually the 911 caller in this situation," said Port St. Lucie Police Department spokesperson Brittany McNally. Merritt admitted to stabbing his father with two different knives, which were later found in the kitchen sink. McNally said Merritt revealed he had longstanding negative feelings toward his father. "It was revealed that he had some long-standing feeling towards this family member, meaning there was some resentment that was building up from what was described, and in comparison to other family members, he felt as if he wasn't exactly treated fairly," McNally said.

Police found the 79-year-old victim inside the home with three stab wounds to the chest. He remains hospitalized and intubated, according to authorities.

Court records show Merritt has a violent criminal history involving knife attacks. He pleaded guilty to a stabbing in West Palm Beach in 2012, where he stabbed his roommate twice with a kitchen knife. Merritt is now being held on charges of attempted homicide and aggravated battery in connection with the attack on his father.

cards.body:

Officers responded to reports of shooting activity at 11:35 p.m. on Sept. 27. When they arrived, they discovered two bullets had penetrated the home, including a bathroom. Two spent shell casings were found near the property. No injuries were reported.

The shooting comes more than a week after another shooting at an occupied home in the 3100 block of Avenue L on Sept. 19. A woman and four children were in that home during the shooting. No one was reported injured in that incident.

The Fort Pierce Police Department has not confirmed whether the two shootings are related to each other.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce driver fled police twice, rammed vehicle before bystander tackled him
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce man faces multiple charges after police say he fled two traffic stops, drove recklessly into oncoming traffic, and rammed a vehicle before a citizen tackled him during his escape attempt.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce man faces multiple charges after fleeing from police twice during a targeted traffic enforcement operation, ramming a vehicle to escape, and being tackled by a bystander who intervened to help officers make the arrest.

Leon Kevin Gentle-Coaxum, 21, was stopped by Fort Pierce Police Department officers around 4:45 p.m. on September 25 during a traffic enforcement initiative in the Okeechobee Road and Jenkins Road area. Officers identified Gentle-Coaxum as driving with a suspended license during the stop on his blue Volkswagen Jetta. As an officer approached the vehicle, Gentle-Coaxum suddenly fled the traffic stop. He drove recklessly, speeding into oncoming traffic and around stopped vehicles using the grass shoulder.

Officers found the vehicle stopped in traffic at South 25th Street and Edwards Road and attempted another traffic stop. Officers ordered Gentle-Coaxum out of the car, but he refused and attempted to flee a second time by ramming a vehicle in front of him. An officer broke the driver's side window in an effort to stop the car. Gentle-Coaxum exited through the passenger side and took off on foot.

A nearby citizen intervened and tackled Gentle-Coaxum, allowing officers to take him into custody. Gentle-Coaxum is charged with fleeing and alluding with property damages, hit and run with property damages, operating a vehicle without a valid license and resisting without violence.

hero.headline: I-95 northbound in Martin County reopens after fatal Honda-box truck crash, then closes again
hero.teaser: Northbound I-95 in Martin County reopened Monday after a deadly crash that killed a Honda driver, but the Florida Highway Patrol later closed all northbound lanes again for the ongoing investigation.
hero.body:
Northbound I-95 in Martin County reopened Monday after a deadly crash that killed a Honda driver, but the Florida Highway Patrol later closed all northbound lanes again for the ongoing investigation. All northbound lanes remain closed with traffic diverted to Indiantown Road.

The Florida Highway Patrol released new details about the crash that occurred early Monday morning. A 2027 Hino box truck was traveling north in the outside lane while a 2020 Honda Civic traveled north in the inside lane and approached the truck. The front of the Honda collided with the rear of the box truck, and the Honda became fully engulfed in flames.

The Honda driver was pronounced dead at the scene at 4:05 a.m. The driver has not been identified pending next-of-kin notification.

The 37-year-old Miami man driving the box truck was not injured. Following the deadly crash, a stretch of northbound I-95 was closed for several hours before reopening and then closing again.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man admits intent to kill father after stabbing, victim remains intubated
hero.body:
A 44-year-old Port St. Lucie man admitted to authorities that he wanted to kill his father after stabbing the 79-year-old man three times in the chest on Sunday, according to Port St. Lucie police. The victim remains hospitalized and intubated.

Officers arrested Cartavion Merritt at a home on NW Blackbird Drive after he called 911 himself, Port St. Lucie Police Department spokesperson Brittany McNally said. Merritt admitted to stabbing his father with two different knives, which were later found in the kitchen sink.

McNally said Merritt told police he had long-standing feelings toward his father, with resentment building up over time. Merritt felt he was not treated fairly in comparison to other family members, McNally said.

Police found the victim inside the home with three stab wounds to the chest. Court records show Merritt pleaded guilty to a stabbing in West Palm Beach in 2012, where he stabbed his roommate twice with a kitchen knife.

Merritt is being held on charges of attempted homicide and aggravated battery.

"Our suspect was actually the 911 caller in this situation," said Port St. Lucie Police Department spokesperson Brittany McNally. McNally said Merritt admitted to stabbing his father with two different knives, which were later found in the kitchen sink. "It was revealed that he had some long-standing feeling towards this family member, meaning there was some resentment that was building up from what was described, and in comparison to other family members, he felt as if he wasn't exactly treated fairly," McNally said. Police found the 79-year-old victim inside the home with three stab wounds to the chest. He remains hospitalized and intubated, according to authorities. Court records show Merritt pleaded guilty to a stabbing in West Palm Beach in 2012, where officials said he stabbed his roommate twice with a kitchen knife. Merritt is being held on charges of attempted homicide and aggravated battery.

cards.teaser: A construction truck crashed through a guardrail and caught fire on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County on Monday afternoon, shutting down all southbound lanes for nearly an hour. The driver escaped before the truck was fully engulfed.
cards.body:
A construction truck crashed through a guardrail and burst into flames on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County on Monday afternoon, shutting down all southbound lanes for nearly an hour.

The crash happened just before 4 p.m. near mile marker 162, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The truck hit and broke through the guardrail before ending up in the bushes and bursting into flames due to a gas leak.

The driver was able to get out before the truck was fully engulfed, according to FHP. St. Lucie County Fire District crews responded to the scene and put out the smoke and flames.

All southbound lanes were blocked at the time of the crash. As of Monday evening, only the left lane had been reopened for drivers to move around the crash. FHP said a tow truck was called and is working on removing the construction truck.

cards.headline: Jury selection begins in Fort Pierce corruption trial of ex-city manager Nick Mimms
cards.teaser: Jury selection opened Monday in the trial of former Fort Pierce city manager Nicholas Mimms, who faces bid tampering and official misconduct charges related to city-owned properties.
cards.body:
Jury selection began Monday in the trial of former Fort Pierce city manager Nicholas Mimms, who is accused of bid tampering and official misconduct related to city-owned properties. Judge Michael Lynn oversaw the process at the St. Lucie County Courthouse, where 60 potential jurors were considered. Several individuals were not selected because they either knew Mimms, had worked with him, or cited medical or financial hardships.

Mimms is facing allegations of using his position to manipulate a bidding process involving two vacant city-owned lots in Fort Pierce's Lincoln Park area. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms ensured that a nonprofit organization called Lincoln Park Young Professionals received a lease to develop the two properties. FDLE investigators said the nonprofit was formed by Mimms' niece.

The trial is expected to last two weeks.

hero.headline: I-95 North in Martin County reopens after fatal crash involving sedan, box truck
hero.teaser: A deadly crash Monday morning shut down Interstate 95 North in Martin County for more than seven hours. The collision at mile marker 91 killed the driver of a Honda Civic that collided with a box truck.
hero.body:
Interstate 95 North in Martin County reopened Monday morning after a fatal crash shut down all northbound lanes for more than seven hours.

The crash occurred around 3:40 a.m. at mile marker 91, involving a Honda Civic and a Hino box truck. According to the Florida Highway Patrol, both vehicles were traveling northbound when the Honda Civic collided with the rear of the box truck in the outside lane. The sedan lodged underneath the back of the box truck and engulfed in flames. Despite lifesaving efforts, the Honda driver was pronounced deceased on scene. The box truck driver was not injured in the crash.

All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed until just before 11 a.m. The Florida Highway Patrol has not identified the deceased driver.

According to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP), both vehicles were traveling northbound when the Honda Civic collided with the rear of the box truck in the outside lane.
