hero.headline: Martin County hoarding rescues raise questions about prevention limits
hero.body:
Two high-profile animal hoarding rescues in Martin County this summer prompted questions about whether more can be done to prevent neglect before it reaches crisis levels, but experts say Fourth Amendment protections and the difficulty of crafting legislation make prevention complicated.

Martin County deputies rescued more than 100 cats and dogs from a house near Hobe Sound on July 20. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek called it the worst animal hoarding case he had seen. Exactly three weeks later on Aug. 10, the same group of deputies rescued 36 border collies from a Palm City house piled with feces and rot. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said that second case was the worst hoarding case they had ever seen.

Budensiek addressed the constitutional limitation when a neighbor raised concerns about the border collies at a community meeting. "There's laws and case law that say you can go this far and you can go no further unless you have probable cause," Budensiek said. The Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures remains a major obstacle to earlier intervention.

Kate MacFall, the Florida state director for Humane World for Animals, said legislators are filing more animal bills and Florida has made progress in recent years. But preventing hoarding cases specifically is more complicated, she said. "It's a bigger picture question," MacFall said. Cesar Perea, vice president of the American Humane Society, said legislation can create unintended consequences. "A lot of times with legislation you create unintended consequences, so you have to be really careful," Perea said.

Perea said cases like the Martin County rescues are common throughout the country. "Unfortunately, it's really common throughout the country to see this level of neglect going on," Perea said. He said hoarding cases typically start with good intentions in breeding or rescue operations that eventually go wrong. Perea said he does not believe the number of cases is growing, but that public awareness is increasing through social media.

Some policy efforts are underway. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, has expressed interest in a mandatory breeder registry. Palm Beach County commissioners are expected to consider higher fees and mandatory inspections for hobby breeders later this fall. For now, advocates say individual action remains the most effective tool. "If you see something, say something. I mean, that's for a reason," MacFall said.

cards.headline: Indiantown-area barn fire destroys building, 6 vehicles; firefighter hospitalized
cards.teaser: A barn fire on a Martin County ranch Thursday evening destroyed the structure and about six vehicles. One firefighter was taken to the hospital with minor overexertion symptoms.
cards.body:
A barn fire on a ranch in the 13000 block of Southwest Allapattah Road near Indiantown destroyed the structure and about six vehicles Thursday evening, according to Martin County Fire Rescue.

The fire occurred at about 5:30 p.m. and sent large flames and black smoke into the air that could be seen for miles. The barn and about six vehicles were a total loss, including a side-by-side and a small front-loader tractor. No horses or residents were injured. One firefighter was taken to the hospital with minor overexertion symptoms but was released Friday morning.

Southwest Allapattah Road reopened after earlier closures. The State Fire Marshal is investigating the cause of the blaze.

hero.headline: Parking dispute led to Pollo Tropical shooting in Port St. Lucie, witnesses say
hero.body:
A shooting at a Pollo Tropical in Port St. Lucie last weekend began as a dispute over a parking space, according to witness accounts in the incident report. Christopher Harris, 37, was shot in the chest but now faces charges of battery and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon despite being listed as a victim in the report.

Multiple witnesses gave conflicting accounts of the confrontation. One witness sitting at a table inside the restaurant told police he saw Harris push another man outside and heard a verbal argument before the man discharged a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris then came back inside and asked someone to call 911.

Another witness picking up an Uber order said she saw a man pull into a parking space before another vehicle pulled into the space in front of them. She said the man began yelling, and as she exited Pollo Tropical, she observed the man following someone out, calling them names and lunging toward them. The witness said she observed something in the man's hand and saw him lunge so close to the other person that they were almost touching before the other person pulled out a firearm and shot.

A witness picking up a DoorDash order said Harris came into Pollo Tropical yelling at another man over a parking space. The witness said the man exited to get his order, and Harris continued to yell, telling the man to come outside. Harris held the door open and then approached the man before the witness heard a gunshot. The witness said the man stated that Harris ran up on him with a knife.

Officers recovered a 9mm handgun from the scene. The Port St. Lucie Police Department confirmed that Harris faces charges of battery and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon.

hero.headline: Martin, St. Lucie, Palm Beach voters to decide eight local ballot questions Nov. 3
hero.body:
Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments. Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Lucie and designated portions of St. Lucie County.

Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds, repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens, expand sports complexes, improve beach access and trail connections, and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities, also repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County's existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending.

Martin County's local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve.

St. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Port St. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee. The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents' preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. The third St. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy.

"It's typically well-intentioned, whether it's a breeding operation or a rescue operation that just eventually just goes wrong," Perea said. "A lot of times with legislation you create unintended consequences, so you have to be really careful."

Some policy efforts are underway. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, has expressed interest in a mandatory breeder registry. Palm Beach County commissioners are expected to consider higher fees and mandatory inspections for hobby breeders later this fall. Kate MacFall, the Florida state director for Humane World for Animals, said legislators are filing more animal bills but acknowledged that preventing hoarding cases specifically is complicated. "It's a bigger picture question," MacFall said. For now, advocates say individual action remains the most effective tool. "If you see something, say something," MacFall said.

Perea said he does not believe the number of cases is necessarily growing but that public awareness is. "I don't know if it's so much these cases are increasing. I think a lot of it has to do with awareness. I think with social media and people being involved, I think we're experiencing like a renaissance of people just not standing for it," Perea said.

cards.headline: Indiantown-area barn fire destroys building, 6 vehicles; firefighter injured
cards.teaser: A barn fire Thursday evening in the 13000 block of Southwest Allapattah Road near Indiantown destroyed the building and about six vehicles. One firefighter was hospitalized with minor overexertion symptoms.
cards.body:
A barn fire Thursday evening in the 13000 block of Southwest Allapattah Road near Indiantown destroyed the building and about six vehicles, Martin County Fire Rescue reported.

The fire broke out at about 5:30 p.m. on a ranch and sent large flames and black smoke into the air that could be seen for miles. The barn and about six vehicles were a total loss, including a side-by-side and a small front-loader tractor. No horses or residents were injured.

One firefighter was taken to the hospital with minor overexertion symptoms but was released Friday morning. Southwest Allapattah Road is back open after earlier closures. The State Fire Marshal is investigating the cause of the blaze.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce brothers killed in Georgia shooting; 18-year-old arrested after altercation
hero.teaser: The Fort Pierce community is raising money to bring home two brothers, ages 11 and 12, who were shot and killed Sunday in DeKalb County, Georgia. Police arrested an 18-year-old suspect and said the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began during a backyard football game days earlier.
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce community is raising money to bring home two brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the deaths of 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark.

According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys said the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident and both survived. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday.

The brothers grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt said both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother said they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family.

A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida to be laid to rest. DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said no family should have to endure the senseless loss of children. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. Padrick said two children should still be alive today. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support as the investigation continues in Georgia.

Their mother also told WPBF 25 News they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family. cards.headline: Fort Pierce police link three Avenue L shootings that struck occupied homes
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects.

The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. No one was hurt, but several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Evidence shows all three shootings are related, police said.

"The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold."

Officers responded to one home around 9:07 p.m. Friday and found multiple bullet holes outside, with several rounds entering through walls and windows. At least 10 bullet holes were visible in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said bullets entered her teenage son's bedroom. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," she said.

She said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." The family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire.

A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on the side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit."

The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said she plans to move her family out of the neighborhood. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. "Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me."

Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.
